commits.pr_title: [Bugfix] Fuse GLM-5.3 KDA q|k|v convs into one conv1d parameter
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

`Glm5NextLinearAttention` cached the merged q|k|v conv weight on the first forward, so an RL refit left the conv kernels reading stale values (#55087). This PR replaces the three `q/k/v_conv1d` modules with a single `conv1d` parameter of shape `[3 * C_local, 1, K]`, which the kernels read directly. Checkpoint `q_conv1d` / `k_conv1d` / `v_conv1d` weights load into it as shards 0/1/2 through `stacked_params_mapping`, using the `_make_fused_conv1d_weight_loader` already used by Kimi-Linear KDA and OLMo-Hybrid GDN. There is no second tensor to keep in sync, so every write path lands in the tensor the kernels read, at a fixed address.

Alternative fixes for the same issue: #56298 and #57638 (see Details; their authors are co-authors on the commit). The fused-parameter design was suggested by hao-aaron in review and replaces this PR's first approach (parameter views into a merged buffer), which broke under weight offloading and `ipc_cache` copy mode.

## Claims

- After `load_weights` / `reload_weights` (checkpoint or kernel format), GLM-5.3 KDA decode uses the refitted conv weights, in eager mode **and** with the default `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE` cudagraphs.
- The conv weight keeps its address across refits, so FULL decode graphs captured before a refit stay valid.
- Works with `--cpu-offload-gb` (with and without refit) and with `--load-format ipc_cache` in both `copy` and `zero_copy` modes.
- No numerical change: the per-rank layout is `[q_r | k_r | v_r]`, the same as the old `torch.cat`. Direct-load outputs are identical to `main`. One copy of the conv weights is dropped.

## Validation

Hardware: GB300 (SM100), TP1, 4-layer pruned GLM-5.3-Flash at full width (`JaredforReal/GLM-5.3-Flash-4L`).

```
pytest tests/models/glm5next/test_kda_conv_weight_refit.py tests/models/glm5next/test_kda_recurrent.py -v
```

- Unit tests (CPU, `conv1d` sub-module): checkpoint q/k/v shards (2D and 3D) land in q|k|v order; `load_weights`-style refit and a real `initialize_layerwise_reload` / `finalize_layerwise_reload` cycle update the weight without moving it. 22 passed with `test_kda_recurrent.py`.
- `test_refit_reaches_cudagraph_decode[cpu_offload_gb=0|10]` (pruned model, default cudagraphs, one engine per case): direct load -> reference tokens; `reload_weights` of the checkpoint with the conv weights x2 -> output changes; checkpoint as-is -> == reference; kernel-format `reload_weights(is_checkpoint_format=False)` on `conv1d.weight` x2 / x0.5 -> changes / == reference; the conv weight address is identical after all four refits. 2 passed (~5 min each, mostly startup). On `main` the first refit step fails (#55087).
- `pre-commit run` on the changed files: passed (ruff, mypy, SPDX, test tethering).

CI note: the e2e test is the first in `tests/models/glm5next` to use the pruned checkpoint (19 GB download, needs SM90/SM100, skipped elsewhere). It runs in the existing `glm5next-unit-tests` step; the two offload cases take about 10 min together on GB300, mostly engine startup. #57537 adds a dedicated step for pruned-checkpoint e2e tests that this test could move to once it lands.

Full refit flow, 3 prompts x 24 greedy tokens, compared with `main` direct load:

| tree | config | direct load | dummy -> `reload_weights()` | `load_weights` partial update / kernel-format refit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| main | cudagraphs | reference | wrong (#55087) | wrong |
| previous revision (buffer views) | cudagraphs | == main | == main | == main |
| previous revision (buffer views) | `cpu_offload_gb=10` | **wrong** | – | – |
| this PR | cudagraphs | == main | == main | == main |
| this PR | eager | == main | == main | == main |
| this PR | `cpu_offload_gb=10` | == main | – | – |

After the reload, every language-model parameter and buffer checksum equals a fresh load.

`--load-format ipc_cache` (a `vllm preload` daemon per GPU, default cudagraphs). After each refit the check compares the conv weight the kernel reads against the checkpoint × scale (max abs diff), then compares the output:

| tree | mode | load | kernel-format refit x2 / x1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| main | copy | == main | weight stale (diff 0.72), output unchanged (#55087) |
| previous revision (buffer views) | copy | == main | **weight stale (diff 0.72), output unchanged** |
| previous revision (buffer views) | zero_copy | == main | diff 0, output changes / == main |
| this PR | copy | == main | diff 0, output changes / == main, address unchanged |
| this PR | zero_copy | == main | diff 0, output changes / == main, address unchanged |

Checkpoint-format refits are not supported on an `ipc_cache`-loaded model on `main` either, so they're not compared here. `_apply_entries` re-registers every parameter as a plain `nn.Parameter` (399/399 lose `weight_loader`), so `load_weights` of any stacked weight raises `AttributeError` (verified on `main` with `self_attn.q_proj`), and the layerwise `reload_weights` fails with `Cannot copy out of meta tensor`. On `main` the three conv weights happened to fall through to `default_weight_loader`; with this PR they're stacked like the other projections. Making checkpoint-format refit work after `ipc_cache` is a separate issue.

## Details

**Root cause.** The KDA layer runs one causal conv over the concatenated q|k|v channels. The merged weight was built lazily on the first forward with `torch.cat` and cached, so later writes to `q/k/v_conv1d.weight` (RL refit through the weight-transfer engines, `reload_weights`, or kernel-format `copy_`) never reached it.

**Why not invalidate the cache (#56298, #57638).** Both PRs drop the cached tensor on refit and rebuild it on the next forward. That works with `enforce_eager=True`, but with the default `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE` cudagraphs the KDA forward is captured inside the FULL decode graphs, which keep the old tensor's address, so decode replays never see the rebuilt weight.

**Why one parameter instead of views into a merged buffer.** Views only hold while nothing replaces a parameter's storage. The UVA and prefetch CPU offloaders set each parameter's `.data` right after the layer is built, and the `ipc_cache` loader in copy mode clones every entry separately; either way the three weights stop aliasing the tensor the kernels read. With a single parameter, those paths, the layerwise reload, and kernel-format `copy_` all write the tensor the kernels use. This matches how Kimi-Linear and OLMo-Hybrid already store their fused short convs.

**Trade-offs.**
- The vLLM parameter name changes from `q/k/v_conv1d.weight` to `conv1d.weight`. Checkpoint-format updates keep the HF names and go through the stacked mapping. Kernel-format writers need the fused name, and GLM-5.3 artifacts saved with vLLM parameter names (`sharded_state`, vLLM-serialized tensorizer) before this change will not load.
- Open PRs #59304 (KCP) and #57496 (CPU KDA backend) reference `q_conv1d` / `_merged_conv_weight` and will need a small rebase.

**Not covered here.** The TP2 cudagraph reload drift from the FlashInfer TRT-LLM FP8 MoE `gemm1_clamp_limit` tensor and the DSA indexer's lazily cached `_wp_fp32` are separate issues, left for follow-ups.

AI assistance (Claude Code) was used for the investigation and the draft of the change; every line was reviewed and the runs above were executed by the submitter.

commits.pr_title: [Rust Frontend] Stream kv_transfer_params on the final chunk like Python
commits.pr_body:
## Overview Python's streaming chat and completions return the request's `kv_transfer_params` on the chunk that carries `finish_reason` (vllm-project/vllm#40186), as the non-streaming responses already did, so a P/D proxy can stream and still get the transfer handle. The Rust stream response types had no such field, so streaming dropped it. This PR adds it. ## Claims - Rust streaming chat and completions put `kv_transfer_params` on the finish chunk, taken from the terminal event. The usage chunk and every other chunk leave it unset, as in Python. - Non-streaming responses are unchanged. ## Validation Commands from `.buildkite/scripts/run-rust-frontend-cargo-ci.sh` (`style-clippy` and `test`), run from the repo root: ``` cargo fmt --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --all -- --check # ok cargo sort --workspace --check rust # ok cargo deny --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --config rust/deny.toml check bans # ok cargo clippy --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --workspace --all-targets --all-features --locked -- -D warnings # ok cargo nextest run --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --workspace --all-features --locked --no-fail-fast # 2312 tests run: 2312 passed, 13 skipped ``` - `chunk_stream_puts_kv_transfer_params_on_finish_chunk_only` (chat) and `completion_stream_puts_kv_transfer_params_on_finish_chunk_only` (completions) drive the real chunk streams with a terminal event carrying params, then check the serialized JSON: only the finish chunk has the key. Both fail with the assignment removed. - `completion_chunk_stream_hides_internal_prompt_only_token` (`echo` with `max_tokens=0`) now also asserts the params on its finish chunk, covering the prompt-only terminal branch; it fails with forwarding removed in that branch only. ## Details Rust already carries the value to both stream handlers (`ChatEvent::Done.kv_transfer_params`, `Finished.kv_transfer_params`). This PR adds `kv_transfer_params: Option` to `ChatCompletionStreamResponse` and `CompletionStreamResponse`, and each stream's `final_chunk` sets it. The value is per-protocol response serialization, so the change stays in `vllm-server`'s stream types and terminal-chunk builders; nothing below the server changes. Known difference: Python constructs every content chunk with `kv_transfer_params=None` set explicitly, so under `exclude_unset` the non-final chunks carry `"kv_transfer_params": null`. Rust stream chunks skip `None` fields (as they already do for `finish_reason`), so the key is absent there. This PR does not change the stream types' null-key policy. No Python test pins the streaming field (vllm-project/vllm#40186 added none). The multiturn disaggregation proxy example reads it from streamed JSON. Not a duplicate: no open PR adds `kv_transfer_params` to the Rust stream responses. AI assistance (Claude Code) was used to prepare this change; the human submitter reviewed every changed line. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) https://claude.ai/code/session_01K2SEJPm2Mawmm6pu8m9E1o ---

commits.pr_title: [Recipes Tool] Fix TP auto-detection for heterogeneous per-layer attention models
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Fix automatic tensor-parallel (TP) selection for models with heterogeneous per-layer attention configurations, such as Gemma 4.

Previously, accessing the global `num_key_value_heads` attribute raised an exception, causing the Recipes tool to fall back to TP=1.

Follow-up to [[PR #60170](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/60170)](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/60170).

## Claims

- Extract attention-head and KV-head constraints from individual layers.
- Support heterogeneous attention models without TP detection failures.
- Preserve existing TP compatibility checks and homogeneous model support.

## Validation

- Three targeted model tests passed.
- Gemma 4 on Xeon 6 (4 NUMA nodes): correctly selected TP=4 and initialized all four workers.
- Gemma 4 TP=4 subsequently encountered a KV-cache capacity issue; DiffusionGemma TP=2 encountered a runtime warmup stall. Both are outside the scope of this fix.

## Details

The original implementation assumed globally uniform KV-head counts. Models with heterogeneous attention configurations reject this global attribute access.

The fix extracts head constraints from each attention layer and uses the existing TP selection logic to determine a compatible TP size. No changes to inference kernels or distributed execution are required.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][CPU] Run encoder-only attention bidirectionally in CPU_ATTN
commits.pr_body:
## Overview `CPU_ATTN` runs causal attention for layers built as a plain `Attention(attn_type=ENCODER_ONLY)`, so EmbeddingGemma 2 and ColQwen3.5 silently return wrong embeddings on CPU. The CPU metadata builder now treats encoder-only groups as non-causal. ## Claims - Fixes CPU output for EmbeddingGemma 2, ColQwen3.5 with the bidirectional contract, and `openpangu` with `is_causal=False`. - EmbeddingGemma 2 now uses `EncoderOnlyAttention`, like BERT and ModernBERT. - No GPU change. The GPU backends already run `ENCODER_ONLY` attention bidirectionally. ## Validation ``` pytest tests/kernels/attention/test_cpu_attn.py -k test_encoder_only_attention_ignores_default_causal ``` - main: 2 failed. 99% of elements mismatched, max abs diff 3.05, and the output matches a causal reference within 4.8e-7. - This PR: 2 passed. `test_cpu_attn.py -k "encoder or dynamic_causal"` (74 passed), `test_embedding_gemma2.py` and pre-commit also pass. Model checks, outside CI because CPU CI does not run these model tests: | Model | Without fix | With fix | |---|---|---| | EmbeddingGemma 2, real weights, x86 CPU (v0.32.0), cosine vs sentence-transformers (text, image, video) | 0.75–0.98 | ≥ 0.99996 | | ColQwen3.5, real weights, x86 CPU (v0.32.0), max change in earlier tokens when only the last token differs | 0.0 (causal) | 0.161 (bidirectional) | | `openpangu` with `is_causal=False`, tiny dummy weights, same check | 0.0 (causal) | 1.4e-3 (bidirectional) | The ColQwen3.5 and `openpangu` rows check future-token dependence and do not compare outputs against a reference implementation. With bidirectional attention, changing the last token changes the outputs of the earlier tokens, while with causal attention it does not. ## Details Both model runners build encoder-only `CommonAttentionMetadata` with the default `causal=True`. `EncoderOnlyAttention` clears it, but a plain `Attention(ENCODER_ONLY)` does not. The GPU backends ignore the flag for encoder attention, while `CPU_ATTN` passes it to the scheduler metadata and the kernel, so the fix is in the builder where both are derived. **Why the EmbeddingGemma 2 change.** The HF reference runs every layer bidirectionally without a KV cache, which is what `EncoderOnlyAttention` encodes. BERT, ModernBERT and the `is_causal=False` paths of Llama, Qwen3 and Gemma 3 already use it, and the encoder-only runner's comment that the encoder builder forces `causal=False` assumes it. This change alone already fixes EmbeddingGemma 2 on CPU: the EmbeddingGemma 2 row above was measured with only this change applied. This is not a duplicate of the open EmbeddingGemma 2 PRs. They fix the Triton prefill kernel on GPUs, while this PR fixes how the CPU backend applies the causal flag, a path those PRs do not touch. **To reviewers.** - The EmbeddingGemma 2 commit does not change output once the builder is fixed. Keep it for consistency with the other encoder models, or drop it? - The new test covers the CPU builder and kernel directly. Would you also like an end-to-end test through `LLM`? The real checkpoints are too heavy for CPU CI, but a tiny dummy-weight `openpangu` model with `is_causal=False` reproduces the bug in a few seconds. ---

commits.pr_title: [Kernel][MiniMax-M3] Add Triton query-tiled sparse prefill tuned on Hopper
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

MiniMax-M3 sparse prefill currently launches one Triton program per query token. Adjacent queries often select overlapping sparse KV blocks, so this PR adds an opt-in query-tiled kernel that:

- groups adjacent queries into one program,
- enumerates the distinct union of their selected blocks,
- loads each union K/V block once, and
- gates each block by per-query membership and causality.

Hopper selects the tiled prefill kernel automatically; other CUDA architectures continue to use the generic scalar kernel. The decode kernel now validates persistent top-k block IDs before dereferencing the block table, which makes mixed chunked-prefill/prefix-reuse batches safe.

This is not a duplicate of the open MiniMax-M3 sparse-attention work:

- #52963 targets ROCm/gfx950.
- #55372 targets query-tiled verify-decode attention, while this PR targets prefill.

AI assistance was used to implement, test, benchmark, and prepare this change. The human submitter reviewed the complete diff and approved submission.

## Test Plan

Correctness (H100 Buildkite):

```bash
pytest -v -s tests/kernels/attention/test_minimax_m3.py
```

This existing H100 kernel shard tracks changes under `vllm/models/minimax_m3/nvidia/` and runs the CUDA parity test directly. It covers partial query tiles, mixed request lengths and prefixes, selected-block membership, non-identity paging, and both NHD and HND KV layouts.

Lint:

```bash
pre-commit run --files \
  vllm/models/minimax_m3/nvidia/ops/sparse_prefill.py \
  tests/kernels/attention/test_minimax_m3.py
```

The one-off microbenchmark harness is not included in the tree. The H200 matrix covers the original scalar, standalone tiled, and PR implementations; tile sizes 1/2/4/8/16/32; six prefill geometries; BF16 and FP8 KV; and 16/8/0 shared selections out of top-k 16.

## Test Result

### Correctness

- CUDA parity coverage is in `tests/kernels/attention/test_minimax_m3.py` and runs in the H100 Buildkite kernel shard.
- Coverage includes partial query tiles, mixed request lengths and prefixes, selected-block membership, non-identity paging, and NHD/HND KV layouts.
- H200 maximum absolute error across the benchmark matrix: `0.0009765625`.
- Pre-commit passed.

### H200 kernel microbenchmarks

Median speedup over the original single tile kernel across six shapes:

| KV dtype / shared top-k | Best representative tile | Median speedup |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| BF16 / 16 of 16 | 8 | 4.49x |
| FP8 / 16 of 16 | 16 | 5.37x |
| BF16 / 8 of 16 | 8 | 1.16x |
| FP8 / 8 of 16 | 2 | 1.20x |

Representative high-overlap results:

- batch 32, q256, BF16: `1.0259 ms -> 0.2252 ms` with tile 8, or 4.56x.
- long-context FP8: approximately 5.37-5.39x with tile 16.

### E2E Prefill-focused SPEED-Bench

A matched scalar/tiled A/B used the full `speed_bench_throughput_8k_low_entropy` split on TP8 H200. Each independent trial ran 512 conversations with fixed OSL 256, temperature 0, seed 42, `min_tokens=256`, and `ignore_eos=true`. Scalar and tiled runs processed identical totals of 2,870,600 input tokens and 131,072 output tokens with zero request errors. Median ISL was 8,223 tokens (mean 5,606.6).

| Concurrency | Scalar input tok/s | Tiled input tok/s | Gain | Request latency | ITL |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 8 | 14,458 | 15,108 | **+4.50%** | -4.29% | -6.35% |
| 16 | 17,365 | 18,248 | **+5.09%** | -4.87% | -5.84% |

### E2E Fixed ISL/OSL

One scalar sweep and one tile-16 sweep were run with MiniMax-M3-MXFP8, TP8 on one 8xH200 node per sweep. The AIPerf workload used fixed synthetic ISL 8102 (8278 server-counted tokens after chat templating), fixed OSL 1024, no shared prefix, temperature 0, seed 42, `min_tokens=1024`, and `ignore_eos=true`. Every request produced exactly 1024 tokens, and scalar/tiled total output-token counts matched at every concurrency.

| Concurrency | Requests | Scalar output tok/s/GPU | Tiled output tok/s/GPU | Gain |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 12 | 36.48 | 36.81 | +0.9% |
| 2 | 12 | 57.16 | 57.63 | +0.8% |
| 4 | 12 | 84.79 | 86.75 | +2.3% |
| 8 | 24 | 118.83 | 123.46 | +3.9% |
| 16 | 48 | 153.29 | 159.76 | +4.2% |
| 32 | 96 | 216.00 | 227.58 | +5.4% |
| 64 | 192 | 264.05 | 281.50 | +6.6% |
| 128 | 384 | 272.83 | 291.35 | +6.8% |
| 256 | 768 | 278.26 | 296.58 | +6.6% |

Tile 16 improves output throughput at every measured concurrency. At concurrency 64-256, it improves output throughput by 6.6-6.8%, average TTFT by 6.6-8.2%, and average ITL by 5.9-6.2%.

---

commits.pr_title: [ROCm][Recipe] Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: add MI355X Quark MXFP4 variant (TP1/TP2)
commits.pr_body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

Adds the AMD Quark MXFP4 checkpoint, [`amd/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Quark-MXFP4`](https://huggingface.co/amd/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Quark-MXFP4), to the [Qwen3.8-Flash-Next recipe](https://recipes.vllm.ai/Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next) as an MI355X variant at TP2 and TP1. It turns on the MI355X work from #59575 that is merged and currently supported by the stock ROCm nightlies.

## Claims

- On MI355X the builder now selects the MXFP4 variant (`meta.default_variant: { mi355x: mxfp4 }`) and renders TP2 for plain TP. The guide also gives TP1, since the checkpoint (169.8 GiB) fits on one GPU.
- The variant's MI355X settings:
  - `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1`;
  - `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_FUSION_SHARED_EXPERTS=1` (#55686);
  - `AITER_USE_FLYDSL_MOE_SORTING=1`;
  - `--gdn-prefill-backend aiter_flydsl`.
- On the stock nightly, the rendered commands serve at the checkpoint card's accuracy: GSM8K 0.967 at TP2, 0.967 at TP1 and 0.965 at TEP8, against the card's 0.965.
- Speculative decoding becomes opt-in on MI355X, so the rendered MI355X commands don't include MTP; a page note for MI355X says why. Every other GPU renders exactly as before.
- The guide describes the MXFP4 flags, the TEP8/TP2/TP1 choice and the validation results in prose, without a launch command. A troubleshooting entry for the MXFP4 variant covers the engine ready timeout on slow TP2 cold starts.

## Validation

**Renderer.** `node scripts/validate-source.mjs --source vllm --dir <this checkout>/recipes` passes in [vllm-project/recipes](https://github.com/vllm-project/recipes) at 05b4c57. At 609f86b, I rendered every hardware × variant × strategy combination with `resolveCommand` from main and from this branch:
- 234 renders are identical, including every NVIDIA GPU and the other AMD GPUs.
- On MI355X, FP8 and BF16 differ only by the dropped `--speculative-config`.
- MXFP4 is new.

**End to end on MI355X.** The rendered commands ran as rendered on `vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:nightly-83c078d955cd6e0c63d3b12abe669c8de936a370` (vLLM 0.32.1rc1.dev361, AITER 0.1.26, FlyDSL 0.4.0). That means the Rust frontend (the recipe default), prefix caching on, empty kernel caches and the checkpoint in the local Hugging Face cache. Each server ran alone on otherwise idle GPUs. On this node each TP2 rank took 380–450 s to load its weights (TP1: 24 s), which puts a cold TP2 start past the 600 s default, so the runs set `VLLM_ENGINE_READY_TIMEOUT_S=1800`. The recipe leaves the timeout at its default, since load time depends on the node's storage, and covers it in a troubleshooting entry for the MXFP4 variant.

| config | cold startup | GSM8K | output tok/s, c1 / c8 / c32 | median TPOT (ms), c1 / c8 / c32 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| TP2 | 622 s | 0.967 | 159 / 801 / 1384 | 5.75 / 7.96 / 22.6 |
| TP1 | 271 s | 0.967 | 153 / 751 / 1282 | 6.02 / 8.77 / 24.6 |
| TEP8 | 251 s | 0.965 | — / 665 / 1831 | — / 8.34 / 17.1 |

Each cell is one run. TP1 was benchmarked twice, and the two runs agreed within 0.3%. The guide's chat prompt returned a complete answer with reasoning on TP1.

```bash
# GSM8K, as on the checkpoint card: chat completions with thinking off, 5-shot, all 1,319 questions
python3 tests/evals/gsm8k/gsm8k_eval.py --port 8000 --use-chat-completions \
  --chat-template-kwargs '{"enable_thinking": false}' --max-tokens 2048 --temperature 0 --max-concurrency 32

# Throughput, random 8k/1k
vllm bench serve --backend vllm --model amd/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Quark-MXFP4 --port 8000 \
  --dataset-name random --random-input-len 8192 --random-output-len 1024 --ignore-eos \
  --max-concurrency <c> --num-prompts <max(16, 4c)> --seed 0 --percentile-metrics ttft,tpot,itl
```

<details>
<summary>TP2 startup on one GPU pair of the test node</summary>

TP2 failed to start on HIP 0,1 of the test node in all 7 attempts, while it started in all 15 attempts on HIP 4,5 and 6,7. In every failure but one, rank 1 died during the last graph capture after the JIT kernel warmup (`Worker proc VllmWorker-1 died unexpectedly`), without a traceback. The exception, the first attempt, ran with the default 600 s timeout and hit it.

The latest attempts ran the same image and command on HIP 0,1 and HIP 4,5 at the same time: HIP 0,1 failed, and HIP 4,5 started and produced the TP2 row above. A Python bisect of df6603f0..83c078d9 on HIP 4,5 started at every step, including at 83c078d9 itself. The failure therefore belongs to that GPU pair, not to vLLM or this recipe. TP1 on HIP 0 and TEP8 across all eight GPUs started normally.
</details>

## Details

- **Speculative decoding** is out of scope for now. MTP doesn't load from the published MXFP4 checkpoint until [its config.json fix](https://huggingface.co/amd/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Quark-MXFP4/discussions/1) is merged (details in #63124). The schema has no per-variant feature switch, and a single-mode `spec_decoding` limited to the other variants fails validation ("every checkpoint must retain at least one usable mode"). This PR therefore uses `hardware_opt_in_features: { mi355x: [spec_decoding] }`. That also turns MTP off by default for FP8 on MI355X, which still offers it as a toggle. A `notes[]` entry for MI355X explains this, and the FP8 MI355X guide section no longer passes `--speculative-config`.
- **TP size.** The variant sets `tp: { mi355x: 2 }`. TP2 matches the checkpoint card's serving command. TP1 is also possible, but since the builder keeps one TP size per variant and GPU, TP1 is only documented in the guide.
- **Strategy.** The recipe's `default_strategy` is `single_node_tep`, so the builder's MI355X default is TEP8. That works since #60816 made native AITER W4A4 MoE the default at TEP8, and it is validated above. DEP is also offered by the recipe's strategy list but wasn't tested with this variant.

---

commits.pr_title: [Perf][Kernel] Add a CuteDSL BF16x3 router GEMM for fp32 router weights on Hopper
commits.pr_body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

On H100/H200, `GateLinear` runs fp32 router weights above 32 tokens as `F.linear(x.float(), w)`, an fp32 SGEMM on CUDA cores. SM100 has the CuteDSL BF16x3 kernel for this (#47973, #55899) and gfx950 has a hipBLASLt one (#52668). SM90 had nothing. This PR adds a CuteDSL BF16x3 kernel for SM90 behind the existing BF16x3 tier.

Models on main that hit this path on SM90 (fp32 router weight, bf16 activations): MiniMax-M2/M2.5/M3, GLM-4.5/4.6/4.7 and GLM-4.5-Air, Hunyuan-V3/V4, Step-3.5-Flash, ERNIE-4.5, Ling 2.0 (`router_dtype: fp32`), and others. The new models are on it too. Beam-1.0 (#62074) keeps fp32 router weights `(5120, 256)`, and Muse Spark Open (#61879) keeps `(8192, 256)`. Both shapes are in the fp32 GEMV table since #62042 and #62126, so on H200 every batch above its limit runs the fp32 SGEMM.

The first revision of this PR used Triton. It is now CuteDSL, like the other router GEMMs in the tree, and uses the `VllmJitKernel` warmup contract.

## Claims

- Router GEMM on 1xH200, inside CUDA graphs with cold L2, over 10 router shapes: 1.6-3.8x faster at 33-512 tokens and 3.3-7.7x faster at 1024-16384 tokens.
- MAE against an fp64 reference is 0.16-0.73x that of the fp32 SGEMM it replaces, at every shape and token count measured.
- MiniMax-M2.5 FP8, TP2 on 2xH200, with main and PR alternating in one container: TTFT 3-5% lower for 8K and 32K prompts, prefill throughput 4-6% higher, and on a mixed 1K-in/128-out workload 4.6% more output tokens/s and 4% lower TPOT. GSM8K accuracy is unchanged and its wall time is 2.5% lower.
- In eager mode one router call costs 17-18 µs of host time, against 21-36 µs on main.
- Beam-1.0 FP8 on one H200, as one TP8 rank (all 52 layers, dummy weights, main and PR alternating): an 8K prefill chunk takes 14.0% less time (155.3 to 133.5 ms), and a decode step at 64 and 128 requests takes 7.4% and 10.9% less.
- On SM90 the fp32 GEMV now runs up to 24 tokens instead of 32, where the new kernel is faster. The GB200 rule for `(5120, 256)` from #62042 and the B300 rule for `(4096, 352)` from #61727 stay Blackwell-only.
- No change for 24 or fewer tokens on the fp32 GEMV shapes, under `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT`, or on other architectures.

```python
"""PR component benchmark: SM90 router GEMM for fp32 gate weights, main vs this PR (1xH200).

main: F.linear(x.float(), W) for M > 32 (fp32 SGEMM). PR: torch.ops.vllm.sm90_bf16x3_router_gemm.
Each number is the per-call time inside one CUDA graph that replays the op on N rotating copies of
(x, W) whose footprint is >= 4x L2, so every call starts with cold weights. MAE is against fp64.
"""

import json
import os
import statistics

import torch

import vllm.model_executor.layers.fused_moe.router.bf16x3_router_gemm_sm90  # noqa: F401

torch.set_float32_matmul_precision("highest")
dev = torch.device("cuda")
L2_BYTES = torch.cuda.get_device_properties(dev).L2_cache_size
print("device", torch.cuda.get_device_name(), "torch", torch.__version__, flush=True)

SHAPES = {
    "MiniMax-M2/M2.5": (3072, 256),
    "MiniMax-M3": (6144, 128),
    "GLM-4.5/4.6/4.7": (5120, 160),
    "GLM-4.5-Air": (4096, 128),
    "Hunyuan-V3": (4096, 192),
    "Hunyuan-V4": (2816, 256),
    "Step-3.5-Flash": (4096, 288),
    "Ling-flash-2.0": (4096, 256),
    "ERNIE-4.5-300B": (8192, 64),
    "Step-5": (4096, 352),
}
MS = [int(m) for m in os.environ.get("MS", "33,64,128,256,512,1024,2048,4096,8192,16384").split(",")]
SCALE = 0.053


def graph_time_us(fns, reps=7):
    for f in fns:
        f()
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    g = torch.cuda.CUDAGraph()
    with torch.cuda.graph(g):
        for f in fns:
            f()
    g.replay()
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    times = []
    for _ in range(reps):
        s = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
        t = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
        s.record()
        g.replay()
        t.record()
        t.synchronize()
        times.append(s.elapsed_time(t) * 1000 / len(fns))
    return statistics.median(times)


def mae(out, ref):
    return (out.double() - ref).abs().mean().item()


def main_path(x, w):
    return torch.nn.functional.linear(x.float(), w)


def pr_path(x, w):
    return torch.ops.vllm.sm90_bf16x3_router_gemm(x, w)


rows = []
for name, (k, e) in SHAPES.items():
    gen = torch.Generator(device=dev).manual_seed(0)
    for m in MS:
        nc = int(min(64, max(4, -(-4 * L2_BYTES // (m * k * 2 + e * k * 4)))))
        xs = [torch.randn(m, k, generator=gen, device=dev).to(torch.bfloat16) for _ in range(nc)]
        ws = [torch.randn(e, k, generator=gen, device=dev) * SCALE for _ in range(nc)]
        ref = xs[0].double() @ ws[0].double().T
        row = {"model": name, "K": k, "E": e, "M": m}
        for label, fn in (("main", main_path), ("pr", pr_path)):
            row[f"{label}_us"] = round(graph_time_us([lambda i=i: fn(xs[i], ws[i]) for i in range(nc)]), 2)
            row[f"{label}_mae"] = mae(fn(xs[0], ws[0]), ref)
        row["speedup"] = round(row["main_us"] / row["pr_us"], 2)
        rows.append(row)
        print(json.dumps(row), flush=True)
        del xs, ws
        torch.cuda.empty_cache()

os.makedirs("control/artifacts", exist_ok=True)
with open("control/artifacts/pr_component.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump({"device": torch.cuda.get_device_name(), "torch": torch.__version__, "rows": rows}, f, indent=1)
```

## Details

**Kernel.** The MMA runs swapped: 64 experts form the wgmma M dimension and tokens the N dimension (32 to 128 per CTA), so small batches still fill the instruction. One TMA warp brings fp32 weight tiles and bf16 token tiles into shared memory. The MMA warpgroup reads each k16 slice of its weight fragment as fp32 and splits it in registers into three bf16 terms. Each term keeps the top 16 bits of what is left, so the three terms sum back to the weight bit for bit. It then issues register-A wgmma against the token tile, and splits the next slice while the current one runs. Products with bf16 activations are exact in fp32, so all error comes from accumulation:
- The first-term products go to a tensor-core partial that starts from zero every K-tile (64 or 128 wide). It is then added into an fp32 register accumulator.
- The second and third terms are about 2^-8 of the output. They keep their own partial across K, as the SM100 kernel does. This is the one numerical change from the Triton revision, which promoted all three terms every K-tile. It makes the largest tiles up to 9% faster. The worst MAE in my checks is 0.87x of the fp32 SGEMM's (GLM-4.7 shape, 7 tokens).

Split-K uses a thread-block cluster of up to 8 CTAs. Each CTA writes its partial tile to its own shared memory, reusing the weight stages, and after a cluster barrier sums one slice of the tile over all peers through DSMEM, in rank order. Results are deterministic, and there is no workspace and no second kernel. There is no host sync and no data-dependent shape, so the op is safe to capture in CUDA graphs.

**Configs.** There is no autotuning. `_pick_config` scores 4 tiles x 4 splits with a fixed cost model: waves times per-CTA time. A wave is one CTA per SM, and clusters of 4 or 8 only fill 15/16 of the SMs (120 of 132; at one CTA per SM, `cuOccupancyMaxActiveClusters` gives 30 clusters of 4 and 15 of 8 on H200). The per-tile costs were fitted to H200 timings. Over 10 shapes and 14 token counts, the rule is within 0.1% (geomean) of the fastest of the 16 configs per cell, and at most 4% slower. Each of the 10 shapes reaches 9-13 configs between 1 and 16384 tokens, at about 1 s of compile each.

**Warmup.** The kernel is a `VllmCuTeDSLJitKernel`. `GateLinear` registers it with its `(K, E)` and `max_num_batched_tokens`, as it does for `ll_fp32w` and as #50177 does for SM100. Warmup traces `dispatch` over 1..max tokens and compiles each key from fake tensors, with no launch. In the end-to-end runs above, the PR arm warmed 13 keys in about 10.5 s at startup. The JIT monitor logged no compile of this kernel while serving; it logged two `fused_moe_kernel` Triton compiles on both arms.

**Host overhead.** Outside CUDA graphs (mixed prefill/decode batches above the capture sizes), the host cost per call matters as much as the kernel. `_pick_config` is cached, and the launch is one TVM-FFI call. Eager host time per call on an idle H200 host:

| | M=64 | M=930 | M=4096 |
|---|---|---|---|
| main, fp32-GEMV dispatch op (MiniMax-M2.5 shape) | 26.3 µs | 29.2 µs | 28.9 µs |
| PR, same op | 18.1 µs | 18.4 µs | 18.3 µs |
| main, `F.linear(x.float(), w)` (GLM-4.7 shape) | 21.7 µs | 24.1 µs | 36.3 µs |
| PR, `torch.ops.vllm.sm90_bf16x3_router_gemm` | 17.1 µs | 17.5 µs | 17.1 µs |

The Triton revision took about 31 µs here. Its GSM8K runs (mostly eager mixed steps) were slower than main by a few percent in some containers.

**Integration.**
- `allow_bf16x3_router_gemm` is now also true on SM90, with the same `K % 8 == 0` condition as SM100. `bf16x3_router_gemm_module()` returns the SM90 module on SM90 and the SM100 module otherwise. The fp32-GEMV dispatch op and tier 4 use it.
- In the fp32-GEMV dispatch op, SM90 bf16 inputs use the fp32 GEMV up to 24 tokens. The `(5120, 256)` GB200 rule from #62042 and the `(4096, 352)` B300 rule from #61727 are in the non-SM90 branch unchanged.
- `bf16x3_router_gemm_cutedsl.py` is renamed to `bf16x3_router_gemm_sm100.py`, next to `bf16x3_router_gemm_sm90.py`.
- The kernel is the custom op `torch.ops.vllm.sm90_bf16x3_router_gemm`, as #55899 does for SM100. The fp32-GEMV shapes keep dispatching on the runtime token count inside `fp32_router_gemm_dispatch`.
- PDL is always on. SM90 supports it.

**Alternatives measured on H200.**
- The Triton revision of this PR. This kernel is 1.25x faster (geomean over 10 shapes and 15 token counts). It is slower only for ERNIE-4.5 (E=64) at 128 or fewer tokens, where 9.6 µs vs 7.2 µs: one 64-expert tile and at most 8 splits leave most SMs idle. It is still 1.55x faster than main there.
- One cuBLAS GEMM over the stacked `(3E, K)` bf16 weight, which is what gfx950 does: MAE 1.4e-6 to 4.3e-6 for the Step-5 shape, worse than the fp32 SGEMM's 3-5e-7.
- A round-to-nearest split, like the SM100 kernel's but without `sub.rn.f32x2` (sm_100 only): 0.5-4% slower than the truncating split at 64-8192 tokens on the Step-5, Beam-1.0, MiniMax-M2.5 and Muse shapes. Both MAEs are well below the fp32 SGEMM's. The other way round, the truncating split in the SM100 kernel on B200 is 0.1-2.3% slower than its own split on the same shapes, so each kernel keeps its own.
- Two bf16 terms (BF16x2): 16 of fp32's 24 significand bits. Even with exact accumulation, that alone gives an MAE of 5.7e-6 to 7.4e-6 at 1024 tokens on the Step-5, Beam-1.0 and MiniMax-M2.5 shapes, against 0.8e-6 to 1.4e-6 for the fp32 SGEMM.
- A pre-split weight kept in memory: needs 1.5x the fp32 router weight per layer (about 760 MB per rank for 88 layers of Step-5). The in-register split needs no extra memory.
- One promoted partial for all three terms per k16 slice, instead of keeping the small terms apart: MAE rose above the fp32 SGEMM's at 33 tokens.
- Two MMA warpgroups per CTA, along the experts or along the tokens (up to 4): not faster than the selected configs in my sweeps.

**Limitations.**
- With one token, cuBLAS's fp32 GEMV is more accurate than this kernel for 3 of the 10 shapes (for example MiniMax-M3: MAE 3.1e-7 vs 4.7e-7). From 2 tokens up, all 10 shapes beat it. In eager mode those batches stay on the fp32 GEMV or `ll_fp32w`. The test starts at 8 tokens.
- As on SM100, generic shapes reach tier 4 through tier 3's Python check on `x.shape[0]`. Under vLLM's guard-free `torch.compile`, that branch can be fixed at the first traced size, the issue #60681 fixes for tier 1. Small batches of those shapes may then run this kernel, which is still faster than the `F.linear` path main would freeze.
- The cost model was fitted on H200 (132 SMs). Other SM90 parts get correct results and an SM-count-aware choice, but the choice may not be the fastest.
- #61727 lowers the fp32 GEMV cutoff for Step-5 to 11 tokens when `allow_bf16x3_router_gemm` is set, based on B300. On H200 the fp32 GEMV is still faster at 16 tokens for that shape, so that rule belongs in the non-SM90 branch next to the GB200 one.
- The Beam-1.0 numbers come from a one-rank proxy with dummy weights. A full TP8 run needs #62074 merged and 8xH200.

**Not a duplicate.** I listed every open PR that touches `gate_linear.py`, `fused_moe/router/`, `fp32_router_gemm*` or `ll_fp32w*`, or that has router/gate/bf16x3 in its title. Most are for other hardware or other tiers: #60376 (SM100 large batch), #60681 (tier 1 custom op), #61727 (Step-5), #50177 and #49627 (warmup), #50535, #61687, #61895, #59023 and #57626 (ROCm), #59486 (quantization), #59925 (deterministic MoE), #37306 (Llama4), #57848 (SM103) and #61463 (ll_bf16 split-K fix).

Merged since this PR opened: #62042 (`(5120, 256)` fp32 GEMV up to 48 tokens and its GB200 rule) and #62126 (Step-5 and Muse Spark Open shapes in the fp32 GEMV). Neither adds an SM90 path above the GEMV's limit. I merged main into this branch and moved the GB200 rule behind the SM90 check.

#49312 (for #49277) also targets SM90 fp32 router weights. It adds an opt-in path (`VLLM_ENABLE_HPC_ROUTER_GEMM=1`) through the external hpc-ops library, with a cached bf16 high/low copy of the weight. This PR is on by default, adds no dependency, keeps no extra weight copy, and its error stays below the fp32 SGEMM's.

AI assistance (Claude Code) was used to write the kernel and tests, run the benchmarks above and draft this description.

commits.pr_title: [Rust][Benchmark] Fix multi-turn input token accounting
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

  Multi-turn benchmark metrics used a cumulative context length that already
  included the current turn's generated tokens as `prompt_len`.

  For a turn with 500 input tokens and 200 output tokens, the benchmark reported
  700 input tokens. Across successful turns, total input tokens were overstated
  by exactly the total generated tokens, causing input and total token throughput
  to be inflated.

  Use `RequestFuncOutput.prompt_len`, which records the prompt length at request
  time, for both overall and per-turn metrics. Remove the redundant cumulative
  input field so the request output remains the single source of truth.

  This makes multi-turn throughput results accurate and prevents longer outputs
  from unfairly inflating benchmark comparisons.

## Test Plan

```
  cargo test -p vllm-bench \
    metrics::calculator::tests::test_multi_turn_metrics_use_request_prompt_lengths \
    -- --exact --nocapture
```

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][Rust Frontend] Decode current NIXL connector stats
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Rust's strict `NixlStats` decoder rejected two fields emitted by current Python NIXL stats. In `MultiConnector` payloads, that caused the NIXL child to be treated as opaque data, so the Rust metrics recorder dropped its transfer histograms. The recorder also omitted handshake/notification failures from the combined failure counter and did not export late notifications.

## Claims

- Decode current Python NIXL `MultiConnector` stats while retaining compatibility with payloads that omit newer fields.
- Record NIXL transfer histograms and align the Rust failed-transfer counter with Python by including transfer, handshake, and notification failures.
- Export `vllm:nixl_num_notifications_after_expiry` from the Rust frontend.
- This does not duplicate [#58563](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58563): that PR adds descriptor-driven metrics for other connectors and explicitly leaves NIXL on its existing typed path. This change fixes that typed path and completes the Rust metric coverage.

## Validation

- `cargo test --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml -p vllm-engine-core-client kv_connector_stats_are_recorded_into_mooncake_and_nixl_metrics` — passed (1 test); verifies the combined failure count and late-notification counter.
- `cargo test --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml -p vllm-engine-core-client python_msgpack_fixtures_match_rust_encoding_and_record_nixl_metrics` — passed (1 test); decodes the Python-generated fixture and checks rendered failure, expiry, and histogram metrics.
- `cargo fmt --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --all --check`, `git diff --check`, and commit pre-commit hooks — passed.

## Details

EngineCore sends `MultiConnector` stats as a map from connector class name to its stats payload. Current Python NIXL stats include `num_failed_handshakes` and `num_notifications_after_expiry`; the Rust `NixlStats` used `deny_unknown_fields` but did not declare these fields. Serde therefore rejected the typed NIXL child, the flattened `other` map retained it as opaque data, and the recorder ignored it.

The relevant flow is: (1) the P/D connector accumulates transfer and notification outcomes, (2) EngineCore serializes connector stats into the `MultiConnector` MessagePack payload, and (3) the Rust frontend decodes NIXL stats and records the matching Prometheus metrics. Adding the missing fields with defaults keeps older payloads compatible. The recorder now groups transfer, handshake, and notification failures under the existing failed-transfer counter, keeps the dedicated notification-failure counter for compatibility, and records notifications received after expiry separately.

The regression extends the Python-generated MessagePack fixture and asserts the decoded fields and rendered counters, including a failed handshake, a failed notification, and two notifications after expiry.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix] Allow pipeline parallelism for Qwen4Exp PLE models and their MTP drafter
commits.pr_body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

Fixes #54709. Qwen4Exp models with n-gram PLE layers (here `Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP8`) refused every `--pipeline-parallel-size > 1`, and their MTP drafter failed on the last PP rank. Since #61016, Model Runner V2 passes `input_ids` to every PP stage for models with `requires_raw_input_tokens` (Qwen4Exp sets it), so the PP refusal is obsolete. This PR removes it and fixes the two remaining failures on that path: KV cache allocation on PP ranks and the MTP drafter.

## Claims

- PP>1 works for Qwen4Exp PLE models, with PLE layers on any PP rank.
- KV cache allocation no longer fails on a PP rank that owns none of the layers of a uniform-type cache group.
- The MTP drafter works with PP>1. This is the second bug in the issue. With PP>1 it also needs #62129 (see Details).

## Validation

Hardware and software: 4× NVIDIA H200, branch head `8d2dd01d18` on top of `b515648641`, Model Runner V2, CUDA graphs on. Model: `Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP8` (48 layers, `ple_layer_ids = [2]`, so decoder layer 1 has PLE).

```bash
VLLM_ENGINE_READY_TIMEOUT_S=3600 vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP8 \
  --pipeline-parallel-size 4 --tensor-parallel-size 1 --max-model-len 8192
```

Before (`main`): exits at config validation, before weights load:

```
NotImplementedError: Qwen4Exp N-gram PLE embedding requires pipeline_parallel_size=1 because non-first pipeline ranks do not receive the raw input_ids it needs. Please run with PP=1.
```

After:

| Config (PP=4) | Result |
|---|---|
| Default partition (PLE layer on rank 0) | `Application startup complete.`, coherent greedy output. Reference for the rows below. |
| `VLLM_PP_LAYER_PARTITION=1,15,16,16` (PLE layer on rank 1) | Serves. Greedy output matches the reference until the first near-tie: 28/32, 4/32 and 32/32 identical tokens on 3 prompts. Max \|Δ logprob\| before divergence 0.11. Needs a local core workaround, see Details. |
| Default partition + `--speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":1}'` | Serves, also with 4 concurrent requests. `Avg Draft acceptance rate: 89.6%`, mean acceptance length 1.90. Greedy output matches the reference: 28/32, 32/32, 32/32. Run with #62129 applied locally. |

The divergences are near-ties. Where the outputs split, the chosen tokens are ` Lisbon` (−0.77) vs `\n\n` (−0.80), and ` <=` (−1.02) vs ` ==` (−1.09).

Unit tests, on H200:

```bash
pytest tests/models/qwen4_exp/test_config.py tests/models/qwen4_exp/test_ple.py \
  tests/v1/core/test_kv_cache_planning.py tests/v1/core/test_kv_cache_utils.py
```

All pass. `test_kv_cache_config_skips_uniform_group_owned_by_other_pp_stage` fails without the `kv_cache_planning.py` change. `pre-commit` passes on all changed files.

<details>
<summary>Earlier validation on 4× A100 (before the rebase onto #61016)</summary>

An earlier revision kept a gate that required all PLE layers on rank 0. On 4× A100 80GB PCIe with the default partition and `NCCL_P2P_DISABLE=1` (that host's NCCL P2P hangs even for a plain `torch.distributed` send/recv), it served coherent output, and MTP reached `Avg Draft acceptance rate: 88.9%`. Without the `mtp.py` change, the MTP run failed on the last PP rank with `AssertionError` at `assert intermediate_tensors is not None`.

</details>

## Details

**Root cause.** PLE needs the raw `input_ids`. Until #61016, the V2 model runner set them to `None` on every PP rank except the first, so `Qwen4ExpForConditionalGenerationConfig.verify_and_update_config` and `Qwen4ExpModelState.__init__` (nvidia and amd) refused any PP>1 when PLE was present. #61016 keeps `input_ids` on later stages for `requires_raw_input_tokens` models but left those refusals in place.

Changes:

1. `vllm/model_executor/models/config.py` and `vllm/models/qwen4_exp/{nvidia,amd}/model_state.py`: remove the PP refusals. The state they guarded (`ngram_context`, query start locations) is built from `req_states`, which every PP rank keeps, and the model forward passes `input_ids` to PLE layers on any rank. If PLE inputs are ever missing, the decoder layer still raises `PLE inputs were not prepared`.
2. `vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_planning.py` (core): on PP ranks without PLE, `allocate_kv_cache` raised `StopIteration`. `_project_kv_cache_groups_to_worker` keeps the global `UniformTypeKVCacheSpecs` for a group whose layers are all on another rank, with empty `layer_names`, so that the worker still has a block size for that group. But `get_kv_cache_config_from_groups` took the layer list from the spec, so those ranks got a cache tensor for `layers.1.ple`, which only one rank has. It now loops over `group.layer_names` with `_get_per_layer_spec`, as `_get_kv_cache_bytes_per_block` and `validate_kv_cache_layout` already do. For every non-empty group, `layer_names` and the spec's dict hold the same layers in the same order, so the layout does not change. Only the empty-group case changes.
3. `vllm/models/qwen4_exp/{nvidia,amd}/mtp.py`: `Qwen4ExpMultiTokenPredictor.forward` branched on `get_pp_group().is_first_rank`. The V2 speculator builds the whole drafter on the last PP rank and calls it with `hidden_states` and no `intermediate_tensors`, so with PP>1 it took the wrong branch. It now branches on `intermediate_tensors is None`, as `qwen3_5_mtp.py` already does.

Tests: `test_kv_cache_config_skips_uniform_group_owned_by_other_pp_stage` is new. The old `test_qwen4_exp_rejects_pipeline_parallel_only_with_ple` asserted the refusal and is removed. The mocked MTP test from an earlier revision is removed per review. The PP path itself is not covered in CI: it needs ≥2 GPUs and this checkpoint.

**Needs attention:**

- MTP with PP>1 hangs in kernel warmup on current `main`, independent of this PR. `warmup_kernels` runs a second greedy pass only when `rejection_sampler is not None`, which is true only on the last PP rank, so that rank waits forever for activations. #62129 fixes it, and the MTP row above was run with that change applied.
- PLE on a later rank for this checkpoint means `VLLM_PP_LAYER_PARTITION=1,...`, which leaves rank 0 with only a linear-attention layer. Startup then fails in `resolve_kv_cache_layout` with `Workers disagree on supported KV cache layouts` (rank 0 supports all layouts, the other ranks `BLNHC`/`BLHNC`). That check is unrelated to PLE and is not changed here. For the PLE-on-rank-1 row, it was relaxed locally to the intersection of the reported layouts.
- `kv_cache_planning.py` is core code. The change only affects the case described in item 2.

---

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix] Keep MRV2 model state in the runtime pool under sleep mode
commits.pr_body:
## Overview Build the Model Runner V2 model state in the `runtime` cuMem pool when sleep mode is on, so its device tensors survive level-2 sleep. Same approach as the LoRA state in #62358. #60009 lists Qwen4Exp `ngram_context_offsets` as out of its scope ("held by non-module objects"); this covers it. ## Claims - **Bug fix:** after `sleep(level=2)` + `wake_up()`, Qwen4Exp's `ngram_context_offsets` (a constant `arange(-ngram_context_len, 0)` on `Qwen4ExpModelState`) comes back as garbage (zeros in practice). Every later PLE n-gram context is wrong, so outputs are corrupted even when the weights are reloaded bit-exact. With this change it survives. - **Scope:** every MRV2 model state, not only Qwen4Exp: all of `init_model_state`'s device tensors move from the `weights` pool to the `runtime` pool. Only under `enable_sleep_mode` on CUDA/ROCm (XPU excluded: no nested pools, as in #62358). - **Cost:** level-2 sleep now copies the model state to host memory, as level 1 already did, instead of discarding it. These are per-request bookkeeping buffers (`max_num_reqs`-sized), plus `inputs_embeds` (`max_num_tokens x hidden`) for models that use it. - **Test:** `test_deep_sleep_model_state` checks that every model-state device tensor is allocated in the `runtime` pool and is unchanged after level-2 sleep + weights wake-up. ## Validation 4x H100 80GB, vLLM wheel for the base commit c9dbc926 (`0.32.1rc1.dev463+gc9dbc9263`, torch 2.14.0+cu130). Each arm swaps in that commit's `model_runner.py` (Python-only change); tests run from this branch's `tests/`. | Check | main (c9dbc926) | this PR | |---|---|---| | `test_deep_sleep_model_state` | **fails**: `AssertionError: {'num_accepted_tokens_gpu': 'weights'}` | passes | | `num_accepted_tokens_gpu` (Mamba2 tiny, MRV2) after `sleep(level=2)` + `wake_up(tags=["weights"])` | all 1s → **all 0s** | all 1s → all 1s | | `tests/basic_correctness/memory/sleep_mode/test_sleep_mode.py` | — | 15 passed, 1 skipped (ROCm-only) | | Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 4-layer slice, TP=4: `ngram_context_offsets` on all ranks, before → after sleep | `[-2, -1]` → **`[0, 0]`** | `[-2, -1]` → `[-2, -1]` (3/3 runs) | | Same: greedy output after sleep vs before (4 prompts, 64 tokens) | diverges at token 0–1, max \|Δlogprob\| 2.29 | same divergence patterns as a no-sleep control (below) | | `pre-commit` on the changed files (incl. mypy) | — | passed | ```bash VLLM_WORKER_MULTIPROC_METHOD=spawn pytest -v -s tests/basic_correctness/memory/sleep_mode/test_sleep_mode.py -k test_deep_sleep_model_state VLLM_WORKER_MULTIPROC_METHOD=spawn pytest -v -s tests/basic_correctness/memory/sleep_mode/test_sleep_mode.py ``` The Qwen3.8 repro uses `LLM(model, tensor_parallel_size=4, enable_sleep_mode=True, max_model_len=4096, gpu_memory_utilization=0.5, disable_custom_all_reduce=True)`, then generate → `sleep(level=2)` → `wake_up(tags=["weights"])` → `collective_rpc("reload_weights")` → `wake_up(tags=["kv_cache"])` → generate. The slice has random weights, so greedy TP=4 decoding is not run-to-run deterministic even without sleep. A no-sleep control (generate twice on one engine, 3 runs per arm) produces the same few late divergence patterns (none, or tokens 5–63) that this PR shows after sleep. On main, every prompt diverges at token 0–1. ## Details **Root cause:** `Worker.load_model` runs `GPUModelRunner.load_model` inside the `weights` pool. `init_model_state` runs there too, so the model state's tensors land in that pool. Level-2 sleep discards the `weights` pool, and wake-up restores only `model.named_buffers()` (and parameters, through the weight update). The model state belongs to the model runner, not the model, so registering its tensors as module buffers (the #60009 approach) does not apply. **Fix:** wrap `init_model_state` in `use_memory_pool(tag="runtime")` under sleep mode. Nested `use_memory_pool` calls restore the outer tag, so the weights pool around the rest of `load_model` is unaffected. Restoring from the pool keeps tensor addresses, so captured CUDA graphs stay valid. **Unrelated, seen while testing:** exiting while the KV cache is still asleep (level-2 sleep, weights-only wake) intermittently logs `CUDA Error: invalid argument at csrc/cumem_allocator.cpp:249` on main too (also with LoRA), from freeing the asleep KV-cache allocation; on CUDA, `_python_free_callback` unmaps asleep allocations. The new test wakes the KV cache before exiting. ---

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][Attention] Keep DSV4.1 sparse prefill out of FULL cudagraphs
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Fixes #59970. Fixes #62417. The five DSV4.1-specific sparse metadata builders declare `AttentionCGSupport.ALWAYS`, so with `cudagraph_mode=FULL_AND_PIECEWISE` prefill and mixed batches get FULL-graph captured even though their prefill metadata is not graph-safe, and the engine dies with an illegal memory access once adaptive verification runs mixed batches at concurrency. Downgrade them to `UNIFORM_BATCH` and report the speculation width as the varlen decode bound, mirroring the reviewed pattern from #59751.

## Claims

- Prefill and mixed batches leave FULL capture for all five builders named in #59970: `DeepseekV4FlashMLAMetadataBuilder`, `DeepseekV4FlashInferSparseMLAMetadataBuilder`, `DeepseekSparseSWAFlashInferMetadataBuilder`, `DeepseekSparseSWAFlashMLAMetadataBuilder`, `CompressorMetadataBuilder`. `FlashMLAMegaAttnBackend` inherits the same builder, so it is covered too.
- FULL varlen decode graphs are kept for uniform batches sized up to 1 + num_speculative_tokens, so DSpark adaptive verification keeps its decode graphs.

## Validation

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/v1/worker/test_attn_utils.py -q
```

82 passed on CPU. The 10 new parametrized cases pin, per backend and num_speculative_tokens in {0, 7}, that support resolves to `UNIFORM_BATCH`, that decode widths up to the speculation width stay graph-eligible, and that one token wider is rejected with the reported bound. Changed-file pre-commit (ruff-check, ruff-format) passed.

Not run: the B300 (SM103) end-to-end reproducer from the issue, no compatible hardware available here, and CI does not exercise these builders. The change only narrows what FULL graphs capture: prefill moves to the piecewise path that the issue's adaptive-verification-off and FULL_DECODE_ONLY arms already exercise for 30+ minutes under load, so no batch that was not captured before becomes captured.

## Details

Root cause, from the issue's arm table: adaptive verification on + FULL_AND_PIECEWISE hits the IMA 4/4 within a minute; verification off in the same mode is stable; verification on with FULL_DECODE_ONLY is stable. The failing ingredient is prefill inside FULL graphs. Each affected builder now also overrides `get_varlen_cudagraph_max_query_len` to return `max_decode_query_len(vllm_config)` (1 + num_speculative_tokens on MRV2), the same width the V2 runner uses when it builds varlen decode replays.

Not a duplicate of #59751: that PR changes only the generic `FlashInferMLASparseTRTLLMMetadataBuilder` for #59681, while the DSV4.1 model wires its own five builders, which the #59970 reporter calls out explicitly. Checked the issue thread and open PRs referencing #59970 before starting; nothing else covers them.

AI assistance: Kimi Code (Kimi K3) prepared the patch and tests; I reviewed every changed line and ran the validation above.

commits.pr_title: [Core][Frontend] Process checkpoint lifecycle with HTTP prepare/status/resume
commits.pr_body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

Make process checkpoint/restore (CRIU plus `cuda-checkpoint`, run by an external orchestrator such as [ai-dynamo/snapshot](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/snapshot)) a first-class engine lifecycle with a production HTTP surface: `POST /checkpoint/prepare`, `GET /checkpoint/status`, `POST /checkpoint/restore`, and `--checkpoint-prepare-on-startup`, in the Python and Rust frontends. Implements the minimal API from RFC #60422 ([summary](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/60422#issuecomment-6187366614)), building on the communicator hooks from #46877 and the paused-request rejection from #51488.

## Claims

- The engine owns a repeatable lifecycle: `running → preparing → prepared → restoring → running`, or `failed`. `AsyncLLM.checkpoint_prepare(mode)` and `checkpoint_restore()` each run as one engine call, so repeated and concurrent calls (several API servers, DP) are no-ops. `checkpoint_state()` reports the state; DP engines merge as failed if any failed, otherwise the shared state.
- `POST /checkpoint/prepare?mode=wait|abort|keep` drains with the pause mode, discards the KV cache and runs the workers' `checkpoint_prepare` hooks. It returns 200 once started (poll status), or 400 with the reason if the engine cannot prepare now, like the other admin routes (for example asleep or mid-cycle).
- `GET /checkpoint/status` returns 200 when prepared, 503 until then and 500 after a failure. `POST /checkpoint/restore` returns 200 when restoring or done (orchestrators redeliver), 400 while preparing or failed. Both work after a restore or in place.
- While an engine does not serve, new requests get the retryable `engine_paused` error from #51488, and `sleep`, `wake_up` and `resume_scheduler` are refused. `/health` keeps its upstream meaning and returns 200, as for a sleeping engine.
- `--checkpoint-prepare-on-startup` prepares each engine once it starts, for capture-at-startup orchestrators.
- The routes exist only with `--enable-sleep-mode`, which preparing requires, as the fault-tolerance and profiler routes exist only with their flags. They document their status codes in the OpenAPI schema.
- The Rust frontend serves the same three routes with the same status codes, bodies and sleep-mode gating.

## Validation

- `pre-commit run` on the changed files (ruff, mypy, typos, markdownlint, SPDX, config docstrings) passes.
- New unit tests in `tests/v1/engine/test_engine_core.py`:
  - `test_checkpoint_prepare_then_restore_run_in_order`: preparing releases the KV cache before the worker hooks, restoring runs the hooks before the KV cache wakes and scheduling resumes, repeats are no-ops, and new requests are rejected in between.
  - `test_checkpoint_prepare_fails_on_drain_barrier_error`: a failing device sync at the end of the drain leaves the engine `failed` and still rejecting, for both an immediate and a deferred drain.
- End to end with ai-dynamo/snapshot (CRIU plus `cuda-checkpoint`) on 8x B200, using an earlier revision of this lifecycle with the same status route, the restore route under its earlier name `/checkpoint/resume`, and `--checkpoint-prepare-on-startup`, restoring into a new pod:

  | Configuration | Result |
  | :-- | :-- |
  | Qwen3-30B-A3B DEP8, Python frontend | Source status 200 `prepared`. After restore and `/checkpoint/resume`: a repeated call 200, correct greedy completions, 16/16 concurrent requests. |
  | Same, Rust frontend | Same results. |
  | P/D over NIXL, prefill and decode restored on different nodes, then a second prefill from the same checkpoint (stacked follow-up) | 3/3 greedy matches per phase, 0 failed transfers, two concurrent empty resumes both 200. |

- The first revision of this PR on 1x B200 (`vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --enable-sleep-mode`, Python frontend), two prepare/restore cycles in one process with no capture, when the restore route was `/checkpoint/resume`. `/health` results are left out of both tables because those runs returned 503 while not serving, which this PR no longer does:

  | Step | Result |
  | :-- | :-- |
  | Serving | status 503 `running`, completion `" Paris. The capital of France is also the capital of the"` |
  | `POST /checkpoint/prepare` | 200 `prepared` (idle server), status 200, a completion gets 503 `Generation is paused. Please retry after it resumes.` |
  | Repeated prepare | 200 `prepared` |
  | `POST /sleep` (dev mode) mid-cycle | refused: `Cannot sleep while the checkpoint state is prepared` |
  | Two concurrent `POST /checkpoint/resume` (now `/checkpoint/restore`) | both 200 `running`; status 503 `running`, same completion as before |

- `pytest tests/v1/engine/test_engine_core.py -k "checkpoint or pause or kv_cache_release or wake_up or reject"`: 22 passed on this branch.
- Existing route-level tests cover the Python routes: the `test_openai_schema.py` fuzz test (the test server has no sleep mode, so the routes are absent) and the `test_authentication_middleware.py` route discovery, whose mock model config now enables sleep mode so the routes are checked as unauthenticated. Buildkite [#97267](https://buildkite.com/vllm/ci/builds/97267) passed all 357 jobs before the Rust routes were added.
- Rust frontend: `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -D warnings`, and the `vllm-server` and `vllm-engine-core-client` tests pass (Rust 1.95). No new Rust tests: CI's Rust frontend coverage reruns existing Python end-to-end tests, and none of them exercise these routes. The Rust routes were validated end to end with Snapshot in the table above.



## Details

**Why this shape.** The pieces exist upstream, but an external orchestrator cannot use them safely: `/pause`, `/sleep` and `/wake_up` are dev-mode routes, `checkpoint_prepare/restore` (#46877) only run the worker hooks and leave sequencing to the caller, nothing reports where the engine is, and other calls can interleave. Moving each step into one engine call gives an idempotent, observable contract that any orchestrator (Snapshot, scripts, future live migration) can drive over HTTP, and that the Rust frontend can call without copying the sequence.

`AsyncLLM.checkpoint_prepare()` and `checkpoint_restore()` previously only ran the worker communicator hooks, and callers paused and slept first. They now run the whole step and refuse an engine that is already asleep. The worker-level hooks are unchanged.

**Not duplicate.** #51360 (`vllm snapshot`), #52132, #35934, #37921, #58183 and #61544 implement checkpointing inside vLLM (CRIU and/or `cuda-checkpoint`). This PR adds no checkpointing code; it is the boundary an external orchestrator needs, and those paths could reuse the same lifecycle later. #48311 owns pause/drain/sleep for RL; this PR reuses `pause_generation` and adds no new pause semantics.

**Tradeoffs and limitations.**
- `/health` stays a liveness check, which the multi-port DP supervisor, elastic EP and the documented Kubernetes probes rely on. A prepared engine therefore stays in rotation, and new requests get the retryable `engine_paused` error until it resumes. A readiness signal that stays false until the engine serves can be added later without changing `/health`.
- With `--enable-sleep-mode`, the routes need no API key, like `/scale_elastic_ep` and the dev-mode `/sleep` and `/pause`. They are listed in `docs/usage/security.md`. A deployment that does not want them can block the paths at the proxy.
- `EngineCoreProc.resume_scheduler` now clears `reject_new_requests` after the base class's checks, so a refused resume keeps rejecting requests.
- With data parallelism, the Rust frontend reports a prepare refusal from any engine, and Python reports engine 0's. Engines that accepted keep preparing. Refusal causes are normally the same on every engine.
- Follow-ups, already prototyped: a checkpoint resource registry for CPU offload and HiSparse host memory (galletas1712/vllm#5), and independent P/D restore over NIXL (galletas1712/vllm#3). No gRPC `Control` methods yet.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][Multimodal] Return 400 for corrupt AVIF and BLP images
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Inspired by #62703. A chat request with a corrupt AVIF image gets HTTP 500, and one with bad BLP data gets HTTP 501, instead of 400. `ImageMediaIO.load_bytes` turns only `OSError`, `UnidentifiedImageError` and `SyntaxError` into the `ValueError("Failed to load image: ...")` that becomes a 400. Pillow's AVIF decoder raises `RuntimeError`, and the BLP plugin raises `BLPFormatError`, a `NotImplementedError`, so both get past that `except`. This PR adds `RuntimeError` to it, which covers both.

#62704 fixed the case from #62703, a PNG with a broken chunk (`SyntaxError`), by adding one class to the same tuple. This PR follows the same approach for the decoder errors that it does not cover. An image over Pillow's pixel limit (`DecompressionBombError`) has the same cause, but #60308 fixes it, so this PR does not touch it.

## Claims

- A corrupt AVIF (`RuntimeError: Failed to decode image: Missing or empty image item`) now gives HTTP 400 `Failed to load image: ...`, not 500.
- A BLP file with an unknown compression (`BLPFormatError: Unknown BLP compression 0`) now gives HTTP 400, not 501.
- Any `NotImplementedError` or `RecursionError` raised while decoding (both subclass `RuntimeError`) now also gives 400 instead of 501/500. These come from the input image, so 400 is intended.
- Valid PNG, JPEG, WEBP and AVIF images load as before. vLLM's own `ValueError`s in this block (pixel limit, decoded-size budget) are not affected.
- A new parametrized test in `tests/multimodal/media/test_image.py` covers both cases and checks the wrapped cause.

## Validation

Setup: CPU only. vLLM at upstream `main` `debcf2284`, Pillow 13.0.0, Python 3.12.

Unit tests:

```bash
pytest tests/multimodal/media/test_image.py
```

With the patch, 22 passed. With the old `image.py`, the two new cases fail with `RuntimeError: Failed to decode image: Missing or empty image item` and `BLPFormatError: Unknown BLP compression 0`, and the 20 other tests pass.

HTTP status: I passed each input to `ImageMediaIO.load_bytes` and gave the escaping exception to the real `create_error_response`:

| Input | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| AVIF with no primary item | `RuntimeError` -> 500 | 400 `Failed to load image: Failed to decode image: Missing or empty image item` |
| BLP2 with compression 0 | `BLPFormatError` -> 501 | 400 `Failed to load image: Unknown BLP compression 0` |
| PNG with a broken chunk (#62703) | 400 | 400 |
| PNG with a 20000x10000 header | `DecompressionBombError` -> 500 | 500, fixed by #60308 |
| Valid PNG, JPEG, WEBP, AVIF | loads | loads |
| Garbage bytes, truncated PNG | 400 | 400 |

`pre-commit run --files vllm/multimodal/media/image.py tests/multimodal/media/test_image.py`: all hooks passed or were skipped.

No model evaluation was run. The change only affects images that fail to decode.

## Details

Pillow has no single base class for bad image data, so `load_bytes` lists the classes. The one added here covers what a fuzz run over the allowed formats found escaping that list, apart from `DecompressionBombError`:

- `RuntimeError` comes from the C AVIF decoder (`_avif.AvifDecoder`) in `Image.open()`.
- It also covers `NotImplementedError`, which Pillow plugins raise for format features they do not support (`BLPFormatError` is one), and `RecursionError` from deeply nested input.
- Every call in this block only decodes client-supplied bytes, so all of these are client errors and map to 400. A 501 in vLLM means the model does not support the API, which does not fit a bad image.

`MemoryError` is still not caught and still gives 500.

This PR and #60308 both extend the same tuple, so whichever merges second needs a one-line rebase.

commits.pr_title: [Rust Frontend] Report the engine's VllmConfig in /server_info
commits.pr_body:
## Overview Python's `GET /server_info` (dev mode) returns the API server's `VllmConfig`, synced from every engine's ready response. The Rust frontend returns its own frontend `Config` under the same key, which has no `model_config`, `cache_config` or `parallel_config`, so the DP `server_info` tests (`v1/distributed/test_{internal,external,hybrid}_lb_dp.py -k server_info`) fail under Rust with `KeyError: 'parallel_config'`. This PR has each engine send its `VllmConfig` dump in the ready response (dev mode only), and the Rust `/server_info` reports it with the API-server view applied. ## Claims - Under the Rust frontend, `/server_info` returns `vllm_config` in the shape Python returns, with the fields Python's API server derives from its engines (`data_parallel_size`, summed `num_gpu_blocks`, minimum `max_model_len`, common `effective_attention_block_size`, `_api_process_count`/`_api_process_rank`). - The Rust frontend's own config moves to a separate `rust_frontend_config` key. - Outside `VLLM_SERVER_DEV_MODE`, engines do no extra work: the ready-response field stays `None`. ## Validation Commands from `.buildkite/scripts/run-rust-frontend-cargo-ci.sh` (`style-clippy` and `test`), run from the repo root: ``` cargo fmt --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --all -- --check # ok cargo sort --workspace --check rust # ok cargo deny --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --config rust/deny.toml check bans # ok cargo clippy --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --workspace --all-targets --all-features --locked -- -D warnings # ok cargo nextest run --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --workspace --all-features --locked --no-fail-fast # 2311 tests run: 2311 passed, 13 skipped ``` - `server_info::tests::engine_vllm_config_reports_frontend_view`: two dense DP engines (ranks 4 and 5 of DP=8) report DP=1, 10 and 20 blocks, `max_model_len` 8192 and 4096, and attention block sizes 64 and 128; `/server_info` reports DP=8, rank 4, 30 blocks, 4096, a `null` attention block size and `_api_process_*` 1/0. It fails with the overlay removed. - `python_msgpack_fixtures_match_rust_encoding` decodes a Python-encoded `vllm_config`. - `ruff check`, `ruff format --check` and the pre-commit mypy wrapper pass on the changed Python files. - GPU, one 4-GPU node, `TP_SIZE=1`, model `ibm-research/PowerMoE-3b`, on an earlier `main`. Before this change, every `server_info` case failed under Rust with `KeyError: 'parallel_config'`: ``` # Rust frontend, whole files: DP_SIZE=4 v1/distributed/test_internal_lb_dp.py # 9 passed, 1 failed: server_info[4] DP_SIZE=2 v1/distributed/test_external_lb_dp.py # 15 passed, 1 skipped, 1 failed: server_info[api-4-standard] DP_SIZE=4 v1/distributed/test_hybrid_lb_dp.py # 5 passed, 1 failed: server_info[4] # Python frontend, -k server_info (the engine now sends the dump in dev mode): internal 2 passed; external 3 passed; hybrid 2 passed ``` The remaining Rust failures are the `api_server_count=4` cases: the Rust frontend runs one API process by design. ## Details Rust has no `VllmConfig` of its own. A Python launcher could pass one at startup, but `vllm-rs serve` launches the Python engine itself, and remote headless engines have no launcher on the frontend's node. Every engine already sends `EngineCoreReadyResponse` for post-initialization config (`max_model_len` after auto-fit, `num_gpu_blocks` after profiling), so the config travels there. - Python engine (`vllm/v1/engine/__init__.py`, `core.py`): `EngineCoreReadyResponse` gets a trailing `vllm_config: dict[str, Any] | None = None`. `_make_ready_response` fills it with the same JSON-mode dump Python's `/server_info` uses, only when `VLLM_SERVER_DEV_MODE` is set. The struct is a msgpack map, so an older peer on either side ignores or defaults the key. The Python client ignores it. - Rust protocol (`engine-core-client`): the matching `#[serde(default)] vllm_config: Option`; the Python fixture and the key-drift test cover it. - Rust `/server_info` (`server/src/server_info.rs`): `ServerInfoSnapshot::from_engine` takes the first engine's dump and replaces the fields Python reports from the API server's view, because each engine reports its own values: | Field | Value | Source | |---|---|---| | `parallel_config._api_process_count`, `_api_process_rank` | 1, 0 | the Rust frontend is the only API process | | `parallel_config.data_parallel_size`, `data_parallel_rank` | deployment size, first engine's rank | same as the gRPC `GetServerInfo` parallelism view | | `cache_config.num_gpu_blocks` | sum over engines | `total_num_gpu_blocks()`, as Python sums | | `cache_config.effective_attention_block_size` | the common value, or `null` if engines differ | as Python | | `model_config.max_model_len` | minimum over engines | `max_model_len()`, as Python | An engine that sends no dump (a remote headless engine started without `VLLM_SERVER_DEV_MODE`, or an older engine) gives `vllm_config: null`. Engines started by `vllm serve` or `vllm-rs serve` inherit the frontend's environment, so in dev mode they always send it. - The Rust frontend `Config`, which shares none of `VllmConfig`'s structure, is reported as `rust_frontend_config`. `config_format=text` renders both with the existing Rust renderer, not Python's `str(VllmConfig)`. The engine owns the config and only serializes it; the frontend view belongs to the Rust server's `/server_info` snapshot, next to the gRPC server-info view it mirrors. Remaining differences, unchanged here: - `--api-server-count N` cases expect N API processes; the Rust frontend runs one. - Per-engine fields that Python's API server does not sync (for example `data_parallel_rank_local`, `data_parallel_index`) show the first engine's values. So does `data_parallel_size_local`: the frontend knows how many engines it connects to, not how many run on its node. - `system_env` stays the Rust subset (`arch`, `family`, `os`). Not a duplicate: no open PR changes `/server_info` on the Rust frontend. AI assistance (Claude Code) was used to prepare this change; the human submitter reviewed every changed line. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) https://claude.ai/code/session_01K2SEJPm2Mawmm6pu8m9E1o ---

commits.pr_title: [Rust Frontend] Accept parenthesized and name-only Gemma 4 tool calls like Python
commits.pr_body:
## Overview Gemma 4 documents tool calls as `<|tool_call>call:name{key:value}`, but some checkpoints write the body in parentheses (`call:terminal(command:<|"|>ls -a<|"|>)`, vllm-project/vllm#53642). Python's parser accepts that form and the name-only `call:name` since vllm-project/vllm#53657. This PR brings the Rust Gemma 4 parser to the same behavior. ## Claims - The Rust Gemma 4 parser accepts parenthesized calls and name-only calls (empty arguments `{}`), in non-streaming and streaming at any chunk split. - A body must end with the closer that matches its opener; `call:f(x:1}` is rejected, as a braced body without `}` already was. ## Validation Commands from `.buildkite/scripts/run-rust-frontend-cargo-ci.sh` (`style-clippy` and `test`), run from the repo root: ``` cargo fmt --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --all -- --check # ok cargo sort --workspace --check rust # ok cargo deny --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --config rust/deny.toml check bans # ok cargo clippy --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --workspace --all-targets --all-features --locked -- -D warnings # ok cargo nextest run --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --workspace --all-features --locked --no-fail-fast # 2312 tests run: 2312 passed, 13 skipped ``` - `gemma4_accepts_parenthesized_and_name_only_calls_at_every_split`: a paren call whose string value contains parentheses, a name-only call and a braced call, parsed whole and at every two-chunk split; checks names, arguments and tool indexes. - `gemma4_parenthesized_call_requires_its_own_closer`: `call:set(flag:true}` fails, and `reset` returns the raw input. - Both tests fail on `main`. Python's PR added no unit test; its reproducer is covered by the first test. ## Details Root cause: the Rust header parser (`rust/src/parser/src/unified/gemma4.rs`) read the name up to `{` and required it. On the paren form the call never left the header state, so the request either failed at finish as an incomplete tool call, or a later braced call's `{` ended a garbage name (`terminal(command:...)<|tool_call>call:terminal`) carrying the second call's arguments. Change: the header ends at `{`, `(` or ``. The active call (`Gemma4CallBody`) remembers its opener, so the body must end with the matching closer, and `reset` reconstructs the raw text with that opener. The change stays in the model-specific parser; the generic argument grammar is unchanged. Deviation from Python: Python drops a trailing `}` regardless of the opener, and a trailing `)` whenever the raw arguments have more `)` than `(`, so it also accepts mixed brackets such as `call:f(x:1}`. Rust picks the closer from the opener and rejects a mismatch. No report shows a mixed form. Not a duplicate: no open PR changes the Rust Gemma 4 call header. AI assistance (Claude Code) was used to prepare this change; the human submitter reviewed every changed line. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) https://claude.ai/code/session_01K2SEJPm2Mawmm6pu8m9E1o ---
