commits.pr_title: [XPU][MoE] Resize batched Triton MoE tiles and change grid order
commits.pr_body:
# Purpose

Two changes to the expert-batched Triton MoE (`BatchedTritonExperts`):

- Grid order. `batched_triton_kernel` is launched with the expert id as the fastest-varying grid axis, so consecutive programs walk different experts' weights. `batched_triton_kernel_swapped` puts the tile index on axis 0 instead, so consecutive programs share an expert's weight tile. Same tiles computed, only the program-to-tile assignment changes. It is selected on XPU only, because the reorder costs up to 5.5% decode throughput on H200, so CUDA and ROCm keep the original kernel and the original grid.

- Tile sizes. `try_get_optimal_moe_config` gains an optional `default_config_func`, consulted after the config override and the tuned-JSON lookup, so tuned configs still win wherever they exist. `BatchedTritonExperts` passes `get_default_batched_config`, which narrows `BLOCK_SIZE_N`/`BLOCK_SIZE_K` to 32 on XPU. The shared heuristic sizes tiles for one large `[M, K] x [K, N]` GEMM, but the batched layout runs `E` small GEMMs of at most `max_num_tokens` rows, where wide N/K tiles are mostly masked-off work. Blockwise-quantized shapes keep the shared config's K because `moe_mmk` derives scale-group offsets from it, and configs without `num_warps` (batch-invariant, wna16) pin their own tiles.

`batched_triton_kernel` keeps its source and its position in the file, so its Triton cache key is unchanged and CUDA compiles the same kernel it does today. `batched_triton_kernel_swapped` differs from it by exactly the two `tl.program_id` assignments. `default_config_func` has exactly one caller, so no other config path changes.

## Testing

XPU: 2× Intel Arc Pro B70, TP=2, DeepSeek-V2-Lite bf16, `moe_backend=batched_triton`, base = merge-base `bca7bea24`.

| metric | base | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| serving throughput, `--dataset random` (output tok/s) | 110.98 | 184.61 |
| offline throughput (tok/s) | 128.81 | 170.29 |
| latency, batch size 32 (s) | 105.48 | 79.62 |
| GSM8K, 400 questions, 5-shot | 0.3500 | 0.3450 |

The GSM8K delta is −0.0050 against a one-sigma band of 0.0238, i.e. no measurable accuracy change, with identical total generated tokens.

H200: 2× H200, dp2 with `--enable-expert-parallel --all2all-backend deepep_low_latency`, which is the CUDA configuration that routes through `BatchedTritonExperts`. Decode is ISL 128 / OSL 512 at concurrency 32, base = vLLM main.

| model | base | this PR | reorder ungated |
|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3-30B-A3B, eager | 321.2 | 320.0 | 304.0 |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B, cudagraphs | 320.7 | 319.8 | 303.2 |
| Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, eager | 275.4 | 275.1 | 269.5 |
| Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B, eager | 227.0 | 230.0 | 226.2 |

Output tok/s. The third column is the first revision of this PR, which applied the reorder on every platform: it costs 5.4% and 5.5% on the two Qwen3-30B configs and 2.1% on Qwen3.5-35B, which is what the XPU gate is there to avoid. With the gate, CUDA decode is within 0.4% of main on every config, prefill is flat, and GSM8K returns the same answers in all three arms.

<details>
<summary>Full perf detail, kernel-level isolation and test commands</summary>

Latency at batch size 1 is flat (50.18s → 49.63s), as expected, since one token per expert leaves the kernel launch-bound either way.

`bench serve` on sharegpt improves 90.12 → 159.67 output tok/s, but that workload measured ±15% run-to-run on this node (same build twice: 159.67 → 138.38), so the random-dataset and offline numbers above are the ones I would rely on.

Isolating the grid order alone on XPU, with the same tensors, the same tiles and the same warp count, changing only the program-to-tile assignment:

| shape | expert-first | tile-first | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| E=32, M=256, N=1408, K=2048 | 1359.8 µs | 676.9 µs | 2.01x |
| E=64, M=256, N=1408, K=2048 | 3633.9 µs | 1024.0 µs | 3.55x |
| E=64, M=256, wide 128/64 tiles | 6436.4 µs | 1181.4 µs | 5.45x |

Running the arms in the opposite order reproduces it (302.3 output tok/s over 3 reps, against 304.0 in the original order), so it is not a warmup or thermal artifact.

H200 GSM8K, 200 questions, 8-shot, correct answers out of 200:

| model | base | this PR | reorder ungated |

| Qwen3-30B-A3B, eager | 184 | 184 | 184 |

| Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, eager | 23 | 23 | 23 |
| Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B, eager | 85 | 85 | 85 |

```
pytest tests/kernels/moe/test_batched_moe.py \
  -k "swapped or blockwise_quant_k_tile or td_matches_plain or td_zero_expert \
```

→ 13 passed, 768 deselected.


→ 103 passed, 96 skipped on XPU, which covers the swapped kernel through `invoke_moe_batched_triton_kernel` on the fp8 and blockwise paths as well as bf16.

```

pre-commit run mypy-3.12 --files <changed files> --hook-stage manual
```
→ ruff-check, ruff-format, typos, mypy-3.10, mypy-3.12 all Passed.

`test_batched_mm_swapped_grid` runs the swapped kernel on whatever device is present and compares it against `native_batched_masked_quant_matmul`, which pins the tile→(expert, m, n) mapping to an independent reference and checks no row past an expert's token count is written. It targets the swapped kernel specifically because `test_batched_mm` goes through `invoke_moe_batched_triton_kernel` and so only covers the kernel the running platform selects. I confirmed it is not vacuous by transposing the in-kernel `pid_m`/`pid_n` decode, which fails 2 of its 3 shapes; the third is `max_tokens_per_expert=1`, where `randint(low=0, high=1)` gives every expert zero tokens and the kernel early-exits. A mutation that merely permutes the tile order does not fail, which is expected since a permutation is what this PR does.

`test_swapped_kernel_matches_original_source` compares the two kernels line by line, ignoring the `def` line and the `tl.program_id` assignments, so a change that lands in only one copy fails on CUDA too, where the swapped kernel is never launched. Adding `+ 0` to one copy's `num_pid_n` fails it.

## Overview

commits.pr_title: [Perf][HiSparse] Reduce residency hash probes
commits.pr_body:
Related to #60072.

At top-k 2,048, the resolver can fill 2,048 of its 2,049 hash slots. Looking up cached rows that aren't selected for the current step then requires long probe chains.

This lets the table grow toward the existing four-slots-per-position target, within the device's shared-memory budget.

Default shared memory rises from 26,148 to 75,300 bytes per block. Resident-only calls cost an extra 0.16–0.90 µs in the kernel checks. This is separate from #60103's slot-invalidation and all-resident work.

On **4 H200s, TP4, GLM-5.2-NVFP4**, with 32 concurrent requests, 16,384-token random prompts and 1,024-token outputs, median throughput improved **130.26 → 133.45 tok/s (+2.45%)**. Three runs each ranged from 130.21–130.32 and 133.36–133.69 tok/s. Reverting gave 130.01 tok/s.

This used FP8 KV, 10 GiB GPU KV per rank, a 64 GiB host pool, CUDA graphs, and no prefix caching. The serving comparison predates the rebase (`d61081dc` → `94b81a59`) and used targeted native builds with `VLLM_GPU_SYNC_CHECK=error`. Post-rebase serving, speculative serving, and other GPU architectures haven't been benchmarked.

On the final commit, `b605dfa0`:

- **1 H100 80GB:** 106 focused tests and 4 end-to-end tests passed with MRV2 and GPU sync checking enabled.
- **1 H200:** 18 resolver cases matched baseline indices, ownership, and LRU state. The 4× target beat 2× in every host-backed case tested.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][Kernel] persistent_topk: sync the CTA around radix barrier arrivals
commits.pr_body:
- Sync the CTA before thread 0 arrives at the per-round inter-CTA barrier in `radix_topk`.
- Sync the CTA at the end of each radix row, before it moves on to its next row.

`radix_topk` uses thread 0 alone to signal the inter-CTA barrier. In each radix round it arrives while the other threads of its CTA may still be adding their local histogram into the group's global histogram, or (on CTA 0) zeroing the next round's buffer, so peers can read an incomplete histogram, pick a different pivot and emit duplicate or missing indices. Separately, a CTA that owns several rows moves on to the next one while slower threads are still scanning `shared_ordered` for pivot ties, and the next radix row's vectorized load, or CTA 0's short-row path, overwrites that dynamic shared memory. The cost is one CTA barrier per radix round, next to the grid-wide spin barrier that round already waits on, plus one per radix row. I found both races while porting the kernel to ROCm (stacked on #62298), and I am sending the fix on its own because the code is shared with CUDA. No CUDA GPU was available to me, so the reproduction below is on MI355X and CUDA CI has to confirm the CUDA build and the existing `persistent_topk` tests.

<details>
<summary>Reproduction, tests and duplicate check</summary>

**Reproduction (MI355X, gfx950).** A standalone HIP build of `persistent_topk_kernel` from my ROCm port, launched with the same grid sizing as `topk.cu`. Its `radix_topk` matches main except for the warp-shuffle macro, and the barrier's acquire load is a device-scope HIP atomic instead of PTX. Each run executes 150 random cases (k ∈ {512, 1024, 2048}; widths 32K-256K; randn, near-constant, 4-value ties, mostly `-inf`, all-equal; ragged and negative lengths; 1-32 rows, so CTAs own several rows) and checks every row against a CPU top-k by value set.

| variant | runs | rows checked | wrong rows |
|---|---|---|---|
| neither barrier (main) | 169 | 882,700 | 146 (57 runs) |
| end-of-row barrier only | 169 | 882,700 | 152 (59 runs) |
| pre-arrival barrier only | 169 | 882,700 | 0 |
| both (this PR) | 169 | 882,700 | 0 |

The end-of-row race did not show up on its own in these runs, so I checked it by making odd waves sleep (`s_sleep`) before the tie scan:

| variant (odd waves delayed) | runs | rows checked | wrong rows |
|---|---|---|---|
| pre-arrival barrier only | 32 | 29,820 | 712 (32 runs) |
| both (this PR) | 32 | 29,820 | 0 |

**Tests.** The kernel builds only for CUDA on main, so `tests/kernels/test_top_k_per_row.py -k persistent` could not run here; CUDA CI covers it.

No new test: the races depend on scheduling and do not reproduce deterministically, so a unit test would be flaky.

**Duplicate check.** Searched open PRs for `persistent_topk`, `persistent topk`, `radix_topk`, `topk race` and `persistent_topk.cuh`, and read the `persistent_topk.cuh` diffs of #62936, #55122, #41748, #41105, #58785, #55314 and #52149. None adds a sync before the per-round arrival. #55122 rewrites the tie-collection stage and ends it with a grid barrier plus `__syncthreads()`, which would also close the end-of-row race, so whichever lands second drops that hunk. #41105 adds a trailing grid barrier only for its fused page-table variant.

</details>

AI assistance (Claude Code) was used to draft this change. Every line was reviewed by the submitter.

commits.pr_title: [MoE][Model] Gemma 4: skip CUDA-graph padding rows in the routing kernel
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Gemma 4's MoE routing kernel ignores `forward_context.is_padding`, so the rows that pad a decode batch up to a captured CUDA graph size are routed to 8 real experts each and the expert GEMMs do their work for nothing. This passes the padding mask into the Gemma 4 kernel, as #48979 did for the fused top-k kernels, and shares the mask lookup that two routers each defined.

## Claims

- `google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it`, default `vllm serve`, 1x H200 (80 GB cap): **+19% output tok/s at 9 concurrent users, +12% at 17, +6% at 33**; unchanged at 1 user and at CUDA graph sizes (no padding there).
- Real tokens are unchanged: greedy outputs and logprobs are bit-identical to `main` for 9- and 17-request batches.
- No behaviour change for other models: `fused_topk_router` and `fused_topk_bias_router` call the same helper they inlined before.

## Validation

**End to end.** `main@852989f`, 1x H200 NVL with `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.5219` (80 GB, as an H100), BF16, default backend (`TRITON_FLASH_ATTN`), V2 model runner. `vllm bench serve --dataset-name random --random-input-len 1024 --random-prefix-len 512 --random-output-len 256 --ignore-eos --num-prompts 8*users`, 2 runs per arm, alternating `main` / PR in the same session:

| Users | `main` tok/s (run 1 / 2) | PR tok/s (run 1 / 2) | Change | TPOT p50, `main` → PR |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 189.5 / 190.3 | 189.9 / 190.0 | 0% | 4.98 → 4.95 ms |
| 9 | 840.3 / 841.6 | 1001.7 / 1004.3 | +19.3% | 9.83 → 8.05 ms |
| 17 | 1346.2 / 1338.1 | 1505.0 / 1513.9 | +12.5% | 11.50 → 9.87 ms |
| 33 | 2118.5 / 2128.3 | 2258.7 / 2259.5 | +6.4% | 13.72 → 12.67 ms |

9, 17 and 33 users run as 16-, 24- and 40-row graphs (7, 7 and 7 padding rows).

**Accuracy.** GSM8K (1,319 questions, 5-shot chat, greedy) at 9 concurrent users: `main` 95.9%, PR 96.1%.

**Bit-identity.** Offline `LLM.chat`, greedy, 256 tokens with `ignore_eos`, all requests starting in the same step: 9 requests (16-row graphs) and 17 requests (24-row graphs) give the same token ids and the same logprobs as `main`; `VLLM_MOE_SKIP_PADDING=0` on this branch also matches `main`.

**Tests.** `tests/kernels/moe/test_gemma4router.py` adds a padding case: real rows bit-identical to the unmasked call, padding rows id -1 and weight 0. `tests/kernels/moe/test_topk_softplus_sqrt.py` patches the renamed helper. `VLLM_GPU_SYNC_CHECK=error` serving GSM8K: no syncs flagged (same as `main`). V1 model runner (`VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0`, 1 run): 823.5 → 989.5 tok/s at 9 users (+20%), 1312.0 → 1477.6 at 17 (+12.6%), GSM8K (300 q) 98.0% on both.

## Details

#46428 introduced `VLLM_MOE_SKIP_PADDING` as a `torch.where` in the modular kernel, which every router went through. #48979 moved the mask into the fused top-k kernels and removed that step, so routers that do not use those kernels lost it. Gemma 4 routes with its own Triton kernel through `CustomRoutingRouter`; with a 9-request decode batch replayed as a 16-row graph, each of the 7 padding rows selected 8 experts, so the expert GEMMs loaded weights for up to 56 extra (token, expert) pairs per layer.

The kernel now takes an optional `is_padding` tensor (a `HAS_PADDING` constexpr, so the unmasked path compiles as before) and writes id -1 / weight 0 for padding rows, which `moe_align_block_size` already drops. The mask costs nothing extra: it is applied in the kernel's existing stores.

Other users of `CustomRoutingRouter` (Llama 4, Cohere2-MoE, Phi-MoE, InternS1-Pro, the Transformers MoE backend) route with Python functions and have the same gap; a generic mask there would add two small kernels per MoE layer, so it is left for a separate change with its own measurements.

commits.pr_title: [KV Offload] Expose the processed prefix at request finalization
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

[#51787](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51787) (f12fe10c5c) removed repeated scheduler touch() calls and introduced key positions for request-scoped recency handling. Those positions can include the full prompt before execution completes, so they cannot distinguish the processed prefix from an untouched suffix when a request terminates early.

Expose num_computed_tokens, num_in_flight_tokens, num_prompt_tokens, and num_tokens as read-only ReqContext properties that delegate to Request and stay up to date. These allow offload backends to derive the processed-prefix boundary, excluding in-flight work and the uncommitted final sampled token. Contexts without an associated Request return None. The complete key-position map remains available for outstanding transfers.

Since ReqContext now retains a reference to Request, release completed-batch context references in the async lookup worker before it waits for another batch.

This is separate from [#54979](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54979) and [#43569](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/43569), which address GPU cache registration and rollback, and [#52103](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52103), which carries provenance through stored events. This PR exposes metadata; it does not change existing eviction policies.

## Test Plan

- Added a scheduler context test checking that token counts reflect subsequent request updates and return None for contexts without a request.
- Added an async lookup regression test checking that completed request contexts are released while the worker remains idle.

## Test Result

All 20 isolated checks passed using the relevant production definitions and repository tests.

commits.pr_title: [Spec Decode] Support PCP with DSpark for DeepSeek-V4.1

## Overview
Enable fixed-length DSpark speculative decoding with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash Prefill Context Parallelism (PCP) on NVIDIA CUDA, extending the standalone PCP path from #59857. Preserve compressor rollback states and keep replicated draft proposals consistent across PCP ranks.


## Claims
- Retain and publish compressor ring tails across PCP ranks so rejected speculative suffixes can resume at an earlier position without losing the predecessor needed by ratio-2 compression.
- Broadcast draft tokens and, for probabilistic drafting, their corresponding logits from PCP rank 0 before target verification. The shared DFlash path also synchronizes confidence values when adaptive verification is enabled; V4.1 PCP still rejects adaptive verification.
- Cover PCP2/4, 0/5/9 speculative tokens, ring capacities 8/16, partial rejection, odd/even accepted prefixes, empty local ranks, and decode-owner changes through the existing compressor regression.


## Validation

```
vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 \
  --language-model-only --tokenizer-mode deepseek_v41 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 2 --prefill-context-parallel-size 2 \

```

commits.pr_title: [Perf][MRV2] Stage buffer contents by reference and copy straight into UVA
commits.pr_body:
## Overview Builds on #63210 (typed-array staging in `StagedWriteTensor`), which is the first commit here. Only the last commit belongs to this PR. That commit stages numpy and `array.array` contents by reference, concatenates all staged contents straight into a UVA buffer slot, and has the write kernel read them through UVA for GPU-resident targets too. Ideas are taken from #59908 (@benenzhu) and #62702 (@Juntian777), who are credited as co-authors. ## Claims - On both GB200 and MI350X, `apply_write` is faster than main and than #63210 alone, in GPU time and in host time, across every shape measured. This includes the small block-table writes, where #63210 alone was slightly slower than main. - A numpy array or `array.array` is staged without a copy. For example, mrope positions or a 131k-token `array('i')` take about 65µs to stage and apply on GB200, against 4–13ms on main. - The write kernel reads staged contents through UVA for GPU-resident targets too, not only UVA targets. This removes the per-apply pinned allocation and `cudaMemcpyAsync`. Without pinned memory, the existing `NonUvaBuffer` fallback copies into a preallocated device buffer. - There is no new option. All existing callers get the same values in the same rows. ## Validation **Tests** (`tests/kernels/core/test_uva.py` and `tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_block_table.py`): | Platform | GPUs visible | Runs | Result | |---|---|---|---| | GB200 | 2 | 3 | 50 passed, 4 skipped each | | MI350X, ROCm 7.2.2 | 1 | 4 | 25 passed, 22 skipped each | On ROCm, `test_gpu_block_table.py` is skipped as CUDA-only. **GPU time per `apply_write`**, in µs at p50 (p10–p90 in the notes below), int32 target resident on the GPU: | case | GB200 main | GB200 #63210 | GB200 this | MI350X main | MI350X #63210 | MI350X this | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | block table 256 × 1 | 19.1 | 10.9 | 6.8 | 12.5 | 12.4 | 6.5 | | block table 32 × 64 | 10.9 | 12.2 | 6.8 | 12.4 | 12.4 | 6.3 | | dense 1 × 8192 | 19.0 | 19.1 | 8.8 | 26.0 | 26.0 | 6.3 | | dense 8 × 8192 | 19.1 | 19.1 | 8.9 | 31.1 | 31.3 | 10.2 | | dense 1 × 131056 | 19.1 | 19.1 | 9.9 | 35.8 | 35.8 | 14.7 | **Host time per stage + apply**, in µs (median): | case | GB200 main | GB200 #63210 | GB200 this | MI350X main | MI350X #63210 | MI350X this | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | block table 256 × 1-int lists | 168 | 179 | 131 | 76 | 75 | 67 | | block table 32 × 64-int lists | 177 | 122 | 79 | 81 | 48 | 40 | | block table 32 × 64, 4 groups (fused) | 527 | 247 | 201 | 272 | 127 | 118 | | `all_token_ids` (GPU target), 1 × 131k list | 5413 | 1384 | 1327 | 3009 | 918 | 910 | | `all_token_ids`, 1 × 131k `array('i')` | 4076 | 65 | 64 | 3502 | 27 | 26 | | mrope positions, 1 × 131k | 13097 | 176 | 178 | 11790 | 65 | 64 |
Method - **Builds compared:** all three `buffer_utils.py` versions (main, #63210, and this PR) are loaded side by side in one process, on one GPU. - **GPU time:** 1. Stage the writes; this part is not timed. 2. Enqueue `torch.cuda._sleep` so the GPU is busy. 3. Record a CUDA event, call `apply_write`, and record a second event. 4. Keep the sample only if the GPU was still sleeping when the host finished enqueueing. This measures what `apply_write` enqueues back to back (the H2D copy plus the kernel, or just the kernel), without host launch gaps. Each case uses 600 samples. - **Host time:** median wall time of stage + apply, with `synchronize()` excluded from the "host" number. - **Distributions:** on GB200 the H2D variants are bimodal, at about 11µs and about 19µs. With UVA contents, p10–p90 stays within about 2µs.
There is no end-to-end serving benchmark yet. The gains are on the step-critical path of MRV2 input preparation (block-table updates every step, prompt staging on admission). They are microbenchmarks only, so the effect on whole steps is unmeasured. ## Details - **Buffer inputs by reference.** - `stage_write` keeps an `np.ndarray` or `array.array` as its own chunk, closing off any pending list contents into a chunk first. - Lists still go through `array.fromlist`, and other iterables through `extend`. - `apply_write` does one `np.concatenate(chunks, out=uva_slot, casting="unsafe")`. - Callers must not modify a staged buffer before `apply_write`. Values are cast to the target dtype, and out-of-range values wrap. Both behaviours are documented in the docstring. - `rope.py` now passes `prefill_positions[i].numpy()` instead of `.tolist()`. - **Direct copy into UVA** (after #59908). `UvaBufferPool._next_buf` and `copy_chunks_to_uva` write the concatenation straight into the pool slot, with no intermediate contents buffer. - **UVA contents for GPU targets.** - Before: #63210, like main, copied contents with `async_tensor_h2d` for GPU-resident targets. That costs about 25µs of host time per apply (a pinned allocation plus `cudaMemcpyAsync`) and about 10–25µs of GPU time for the copy engine. - Now: the kernel reads the pinned contents directly. Both approaches cross the link once and run serialized on the same stream. The UVA read was cheaper on NVLink-C2C (GB200) and on PCIe (MI350X) alike, including for 512KB dense writes. - `FusedStagedWriter` gets a UVA contents pool for the same reason. - **No rollback in `stage_write`.** The try/except from #63210 is removed: `fromlist` is already atomic, and a failed staging call is a caller bug. - **Typecode map.** `TORCH_DTYPE_TO_ARRAY_TYPECODE` moves to `vllm/utils/torch_utils.py`, next to `TORCH_DTYPE_TO_NUMPY_DTYPE`. - **Interaction with #62702.** #62702 keeps prompt token ids as int32 `array`s end to end. With this PR, those arrays are staged into `all_token_ids` without any copy. - **Tests.** - `test_staged_write_input_types`: interleaves lists, ranges, int64 and strided int32 arrays, `array('i')`, empty arrays and `stage_write_elem`. - `test_staged_write_uses_uva_contents`: now covers both target kinds, pinned to the target's device. Without that, a leftover current device from an earlier test makes the GPU-target case fail when two GPUs are visible. - `test_staged_write_without_uva`: forces the `NonUvaBuffer` fallback through `apply_write` and through `FusedStagedWriter`. ---

commits.pr_title: [KV Offload][P2P] Fail faster: per-mode load timeout, shorter abort-ack and lookup timeouts
commits.pr_body:
## Overview Part of #63602: the P2P KV offload tier fails faster on a stuck peer. Symmetric-P2P loads time out after 10s instead of 30s, PD loads keep 30s, the abort-ack timeout drops from 10s to 5s, and the lookup no-progress timeout drops from 30s to 8s. ## Claims - A stuck symmetric-P2P fetch is surfaced as failed (and recomputed locally) after ~15s (10s load + 5s abort-ack) instead of ~40s. - A stuck PD fetch fails after ~35s (30s load + 5s abort-ack) instead of ~40s; the PD load timeout itself is unchanged. - An unanswered symmetric-P2P lookup expires the session after 8s without progress instead of 30s. ## Validation - `pytest tests/v1/kv_offload/tiering/p2p/`: 325 passed. - New `test_load_timeout_depends_on_mode`: a probed (P2P) load and an unprobed (PD) load are both backdated past the P2P timeout; only the P2P one aborts. - Not yet validated end-to-end on a P2P / PD deployment. ## Details - **Per-mode load timeout.** `_InboundLoadState` gets a `timeout_s` fixed at `request_blocks` time: `_P2P_LOAD_TIMEOUT_S` (10s) when the id ran the lookup phase (`st.probed`), otherwise `_PD_LOAD_TIMEOUT_S` (30s). A symmetric fetch only goes out for keys the peer has already confirmed it holds, so a fetch that has not landed after 10s is stuck. A PD prefiller may still be computing the blocks when the fetch arrives, so PD keeps room for a full prefill. - **Abort-ack 5s** applies to both modes. Once we have sent `AbortFetchMsg`, waiting longer for the ack does not depend on whether the blocks needed computing. - **Lookup 8s** stays above the producer's `_LOOKUP_PENDING_TIMEOUT_S` (5s), so a producer holding a `HIT_PENDING` key answers MISS before the consumer gives up. - `_REAPED_ID_RETENTION_S` (60s) still exceeds the longest load timeout (30s). - Tradeoff: on a slow but healthy data plane (e.g. very large symmetric fetches over degraded NICs), a fetch that genuinely needs >10s now aborts and falls back to local recompute. The timeouts remain module constants; they are not made configurable here. ---

commits.pr_title: [MoE] Add locality-domain allocation for FlashInfer CuTeDSL NVFP4
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Add opt-in locality-domain weight allocation and MoE execution on Rubin, using upstream PyTorch locality APIs and FlashInfer CuTeDSL. Requires the stream-execution compatibility fix in [FlashInfer #6488](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/6488).

## Claims

- Support locality-domain allocation and localized MoE execution.
- Support optional backfill, overlapping output memset, and releasing full-width weights.
- Use CUDA graph autotuning consistently for localized and baseline execution.

## Validation

### MoE op performance

Measured on Rubin with NVFP4 inputs/weights, BF16 output, SiTU activation, and balanced routing. Both paths independently autotune with CUDA graph profiling—no manually fixed tactics. Timing covers **FC1 + memset + FC2**, excluding routing and input preparation.

Per-rank shapes (hidden / intermediate / experts / top-k):

- **TP8-shaped:** 3584 / 384 / 896 / 16; no backfill.
- **TEP16-shaped:** 3584 / 3072 / 56 / 16; backfill enabled.

Median latency over 10 alternating paired rounds, each with 8 calls per graph and 125 replays. Speedup is the median paired ratio; ranges show min–max.

| Shape | Tokens | Baseline (µs) | Localized (µs) | Speedup | Range |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| TP8-shaped | 64 | 199.163 | 185.427 | 1.074× | 1.074–1.075× |
| TP8-shaped | 128 | 203.928 | 188.833 | 1.080× | 1.080–1.080× |
| TP8-shaped | 256 | 207.981 | 192.078 | 1.083× | 1.083–1.083× |
| TEP16-shaped | 32 | 92.315 | 80.600 | 1.145× | 1.145–1.146× |
| TEP16-shaped | 64 | 92.368 | 79.582 | 1.161× | 1.160–1.161× |
| TEP16-shaped | 128 | 93.310 | 82.644 | 1.129× | 1.128–1.130× |
| TEP16-shaped | 256 | 94.930 | 81.353 | 1.167× | 1.152–1.179× |
| TEP16-shaped | 512 | 128.676 | 126.227 | 1.019× | 0.992–1.047× |
| TEP16-shaped | 1024 | 191.054 | 189.298 | 1.008× | 0.995–1.021× |

## Details

Enable with `VLLM_USE_LOCALITY_DOMAINS=1` and `--moe-backend flashinfer_cutedsl`. Requires compatible PyTorch, CUDA, and FlashInfer builds. Optional controls:

- `VLLM_MOE_LOCALIZE_BACKFILL=1`: enable backfill.
- `VLLM_MOE_LOCALIZE_FREE_FULL_WEIGHTS=1`: release original weights and restrict tuning to localized execution.
- `VLLM_MOE_LOCALIZE_MEMSET_OVERLAP`: enabled by default.

Localization is disabled by default; localized per-token activation quantization is unsupported.

Also includes K3 KDA compatibility adjustments for Triton nightly: remove `B` from `do_not_specialize` because it is not a kernel argument in the NVIDIA/AMD implementations, and align gated normalization with [upstream FLA #1062](https://github.com/fla-org/flash-linear-attention/pull/1062), preserving K3's head-aware, row-strided gate addressing. The block-pointer migration is already in vLLM main; the remaining gated-norm diff only aligns the gate-load expression/mask and records upstream provenance. AMD runtime validation remains pending.

commits.pr_title: [CI][ROCm] Take NIXL PD accuracy side-channel ports from below the ephemeral range
commits.pr_body: - `rocm_pd_accuracy_utils.py`: take each server's `VLLM_NIXL_SIDE_CHANNEL_PORT` from below the kernel's ephemeral range instead of from `get_open_port()` `test_rocm_pd_accuracy[nixl-aiter-deepseek-p1-d1]` failed in [amd-ci 15356](https://buildkite.com/vllm/amd-ci/builds/15356/list?sid=01a1707d-94ec-44ea-af1c-5245434b7339&tab=output): the decode server's `nixl_handshake_listener` hit `ZMQError: Address already in use (tcp://localhost:55235)`, and the server then waited out its startup timeout. The test has picked the side-channel port with `get_open_port()` since #58095, and NIXL only binds `side_channel_port + data_parallel_index` after the model loads, so for ~30 s the released port sits in the ephemeral range where any other `bind(0)` can be given it. This group otherwise passed 6/6 params in every nightly and weekly build from 14934 to 15350, so it is a rare race (about 1 in ~300 param runs) rather than a regression. Ports below `/proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_local_port_range` are never handed out by `bind(0)` or `connect()`, the same approach as #63453 for MoRIIO. Separately, a dead handshake listener leaves the server neither failing nor healthy; that is a product issue for a follow-up. The full CI file passes with this change on MI350X (6 passed; GSM8K 0.412-0.424 for Qwen, 0.195-0.202 for DeepSeek, in line with 15356's passing params). commits.pr_title: [CI][ROCm] Take MoRIIO P/D test port blocks from below the ephemeral range
commits.pr_body:
- `test_write_dummy_e2e_rocm.py`: `_open_port_block` picks its block below the kernel's ephemeral range instead of starting from `get_open_port()`

The MoRIIO dummy-weight P/D test hands each server handshake and notify ports that MoRIIO only binds, plus one port per TP rank, after the model loads. #62473 already stopped the test from handing the same port to two of its own servers. But the blocks still started at `get_open_port()`, i.e. inside the ephemeral range, and a released port there can go to any other `bind(0)` listener the servers start in the meantime (RCCL, gloo, ZMQ). The listener thread then dies with `Address already in use`, e.g. a TP1 decode server's notify port in [amd-ci build 15267](https://buildkite.com/vllm/amd-ci/builds/15267/table?jid=01a167fe-b072-4523-b8b6-522a7cfa0163&tab=output) and a handshake port in [build 96960](https://buildkite.com/vllm/ci/builds/96960/list?jid=01a16a64-0c77-44f1-bcd6-4c5ade40c544&tab=output). The race has been there since the test was added in #60544. `bind(0)` and `connect()` never hand out ports below `/proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_local_port_range`, so taking the blocks from there removes it. #60743 is complementary: it makes MoRIIO fail startup loudly when the bind fails.

Locally, a released `bind(0)` port came back to a later `bind(0)` listener in 26 of 5000 trials with 32 listeners, while 200,000 `bind(0)` calls never returned a port below 32768. The new `_open_port_block`, called from 8 threads, gave 400 disjoint blocks of 8, all below 32768 and none containing any of 614 ports held by another process.

AI assistance (Claude Code) was used to draft this change. Every line was reviewed by the submitter.

commits.pr_title: [CI][ROCm] Skip the AITER MoE garbage-rows test for fp8 per-tensor until the AITER fix
commits.pr_body: - `test_modular_kernel_combinations.py`: skip `test_aiter_moe_token_padding_garbage_rows` for fp8 per-tensor configs until the AITER fix is in the pinned `AITER_BRANCH` `test_aiter_moe_token_padding_garbage_rows[single_inf-fp8_tensor_tensor]` and `[single_nan-fp8_tensor_token]` failed on MI300 in [amd-ci 15340](https://buildkite.com/vllm/amd-ci/builds/15340) with `mean |mk_out| = 0`. The bug is in AITER, not vLLM: `fused_moe_2stages` allocates `a2` with `torch.empty`, stage 1 never writes the slots of `topk_ids == -1` rows, and the dynamic per-tensor a2 quant then takes its scale over that stale memory, which can push every real row to fp8 zero. Per-token and block schemes scale row by row and are unaffected, so only configs with fp8 per-tensor weights (which the test runs with no static a2 scale) are skipped. The AITER fix is ROCm/aiter#6568; this guard should be removed when `AITER_BRANCH` includes it. #62927 targets the same failure from the vLLM side but does not fix it (details in that PR). On MI350X with AITER v0.1.26, poisoning the caching allocator with 1e30 makes exactly the four skipped params fail (3/3 runs) while the other nine pass; nothing was run on MI300, where CI failed (1 failing nightly of ~10 since 2026-10-08). With the guard, the group runs 9 passed, 7 skipped. This adds a skip, which tests/AGENTS.md discourages; it is a temporary ROCm-only guard until the AITER bump, alongside the existing ROCm/aiter#6275 skip in the same test. commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][ROCm][DSv4.1] Await krdy before K2's combine reads klen in index-source launches
commits.pr_body:
- In K2's `stage_combine` (`mono/attention/back.py`), an index source now waits for its token's `krdy` flag and reads `klen` past the per-XCD caches (CM_DEV), as `stage_split` already does.
- Non-index launches are unchanged: both are behind `const_expr("krdy" in c)`.

An index-source K2 rebuilds the key table (`kt`/`klen`) itself in the same launch. #61082 made the split stage wait for that, but the combine still read `klen` with a plain load and no wait, so it can see the previous launch's key count. Whether that breaks anything depends on how the stale count compares with the real one:

| Previous launch's `klen` vs this launch's | What the combine does | Before | After |
|---|---|---|---|
| Equal | Merges the right chunks by luck | Correct | Correct |
| Smaller | Merges too few chunks | Wrong attention output: 3,791 of 8,704 MXFP8 codes of the attention output wrong (`Case(ratio=2, R=17, T=1, index=True)`, TP2) | Correct |
| Larger | Waits on split chunks that are never published | Hang: the unbounded `_spin` never returns (killed at 420 s, 3/3 runs, TP2) | Correct |

That is the index-source failure caught by the slow-reference test in #63486, and the intermittent index-source hang seen while stressing it.

| Check (MI350X, AITER v0.1.26) | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Index-source vs reference, TP2 | 0/3 pass | 39/40 pass (10 + 30 loop) |
| Index-source vs reference, TP4 | 0/2 pass | 3/3 pass |
| Long-then-short index sequence, TP2 | 3/3 hang | 3/3 pass |
| Same token pair, both orders, TP2 | 0/3 pass | 15/15 pass |
| Rest of the DSv4.1 mono numerics / layers / decode tests | - | 7 passed + 1 skipped / 4 passed + 1 skipped / 85 passed |

The one failing TP2 run in the 40 failed the relative-error check before per-row logging was added; the 30 logged runs after it were bit-identical (rel 0.006460). Index launches were not exercised on gfx942, which shares this code.

**Performance.** One layer step (K1 + index select + K2 + FFN) captured as a CUDA graph of 20 steps, 200 replays, 5 base and 5 fix runs interleaved. Each index case runs after its non-index twin so that the stale `klen` equals the correct one and the base result is valid. Median per step:

| Case | Base (us) | Fix (us) | Fix - base (us) |
|---|---|---|---|
| TP2, index, R=17 short | 448.1-450.8 | 448.6-450.6 | -0.1 to +0.1 |
| TP2, index, R=17 long | 451.1-452.3 | 450.7-451.6 | -0.6 to +0.2 |
| TP2, index, R=4 x T=6 | 554.0-557.4 | 555.8-558.2 | -0.1 to +1.3 |
| TP4, index, R=17 short | 306.3-308.0 | 307.1-307.5 | -0.3 to +0.6 |
| TP4, index, R=17 long | 307.6-309.2 | 308.0-308.9 | -0.6 to +0.6 |
| TP4, index, R=4 x T=6 | 366.5-367.8 | 367.0-368.5 | +0.7 to +0.8 |
| Non-index control (unchanged code) | - | - | -0.3 to +0.4 |

Every delta is within the ~1 us (0.2-0.3%) run-to-run noise of the unchanged control: the `krdy` flag is normally published long before the combine reaches it, so the cost is one device-scope poll and a CTA barrier per combine unit.

This unblocks #63486, whose DSv4.1 index-source test is a plain test that depends on this fix.

AI assistance (Claude Code) was used to draft this change. Every line was reviewed by the submitter.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][Tool Parser] Keep Step3 parameter values that contain '<'
commits.pr_body:
## Overview The Step3 tool parser silently drops any parameter whose value contains `<`. This PR makes the parameter regex match up to the closing tag instead of the first `<`. ## Claims - Step3 tool calls keep parameter values that contain `<`, such as `a < 5` or `hi`, in streaming and non-streaming mode. - Values without `<` parse exactly as before. ## Validation New unit test `test_parameter_value_with_angle_bracket`, run in both streaming and non-streaming mode: ```bash python -m pytest -q tests/tool_parsers/test_step3_tool_parser.py ``` | | Result | |---|---| | Before (test only) | `2 failed, 9 passed, 8 xfailed`: `assert {} == {'sql': 'SELECT * FROM t WHERE a < 5', 'html': 'hi'}` | | After | `11 passed, 8 xfailed` | The 8 xfails already exist on main and are unchanged. End-to-end check with a Step3 model (`tool_choice="auto"`, a tool with a string parameter, prompt asking for a SQL query with `<`): Parser check with the real Step3 tokenizer (`stepfun-ai/step3`). A tool call whose `sql` value contains `<` goes through `run_tool_extraction`, the helper the tool parser tests use, in both modes: | Mode | `main` (`arguments`) | This PR (`arguments`) | |---|---|---| | non-streaming | `{}` | `{"sql": "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE total < 100"}` | | streaming | `{}` | `{"sql": "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE total < 100"}` | On `main` the call is still emitted, but its arguments come back empty, so a client runs the tool with no input. Not run end to end: Step3 has 321B parameters and I have no hardware that can serve it. The change is confined to the parameter regex, which the check above drives with the model's real tokenizer.
Reproduction script import json from vllm.tokenizers import get_tokenizer from vllm.tool_parsers import ToolParserManager from tests.tool_parsers.utils import run_tool_extraction tok = get_tokenizer("stepfun-ai/step3") out = ("<｜tool_calls_begin｜><｜tool_call_begin｜>function<｜tool_sep｜>" '' 'SELECT * FROM orders WHERE total < 100' "<｜tool_call_end｜><｜tool_calls_end｜>") for streaming in (False, True): parser = ToolParserManager.get_tool_parser("step3")(tok) _, calls = run_tool_extraction(parser, out, streaming=streaming) print(streaming, [json.loads(c.function.arguments or "{}") for c in calls])
## Details Root cause: `_parse_steptml_invoke` matched values with `([^<]*)`, so the regex failed on any value containing `<` and the parameter was skipped without a log line. The value group is now `(.*?)` with `re.DOTALL`. It ends at the first ``, and multi-line values still match as before. Limit: a value that contains the literal text `` still ends early. The format has no escaping, so this cannot be fixed in the parser. Not a duplicate: I searched open and closed PRs for "step3 tool parser" and issues and PRs for "steptml". #49567 (whitespace in Step3 values) only removes `.strip()` and keeps `[^<]*`. #55115 and #57809 change streaming bookkeeping, not the regex. #55175 changes test fixtures only. No issue reports this bug. Co-author: Claude ---

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][Spec Decode] Preserve DP replica index for standalone draft models
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Preserve the target DP replica index when constructing a standalone
`method="draft_model"` model. This prevents separate replicas from sharing
device-bound compiled draft artifacts and fixes a reproduced DP=2 warm-cache
startup failure. Follow-up to #62285 and the standalone analysis on #62062;
the root-cause analysis and suggested restoration were reported by @Siquan-Li.

#62062 currently changes DFlash/DSpark paths; this PR fixes the standalone
`draft_model` loader and does not duplicate those changes.

## Claims

- Restore the replica index after draft config construction and before loading
  the model. General `ParallelConfig` semantics and sibling speculators are
  unchanged.
- Isolate draft compilation/AOT artifacts by replica. Existing loader
  regressions cover zero and nonzero target indices.
- Fix the observed warm-cache `CUDA driver error: invalid argument`; do not
  claim an accuracy improvement or serving speedup.

## Validation

61 targeted CPU cases passed:

```sh
PYTHONPATH=. .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_model_runner_v2.py tests/v1/worker/test_dspark_utils.py tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_target_dependent_ar_speculator.py -q
```

The scoped regression without the fix fails for the three nonzero-index cases;
rank-zero controls pass. It is part of the existing Buildkite
`v1-executor-worker` suite. Scoped pre-commit checks passed during
implementation; upstream pre-commit execution is currently gated by
contributor eligibility.

[Raw commands, server logs, evaluation outputs/samples and benchmark outputs/per-request JSON](https://github.com/MuonChaser/vllm/releases/tag/pr-62301-validation-20261019).

The end-to-end validation used the public Apache-2.0 model
[`Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B`](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B) as both target and
draft, pinned to public revision
`c1899de289a04d12100db370d81485cdf75e47ca`.
The equivalent public-model reproducer is:

```bash
export MODEL_ID=Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B
export MODEL_REVISION=c1899de289a04d12100db370d81485cdf75e47ca
export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1 VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1
export VLLM_USE_FLASHINFER_SAMPLER=0
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=4 TORCHINDUCTOR_COMPILE_THREADS=1
export VLLM_CACHE_ROOT=/tmp/vllm-62301/cache/vllm
export TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR=/tmp/vllm-62301/cache/inductor
export TRITON_CACHE_DIR=/tmp/vllm-62301/cache/triton

.venv/bin/python -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server \
  --model "$MODEL_ID" \
  --revision "$MODEL_REVISION" \
  --served-model-name probe \
  --host 127.0.0.1 \
  --port 18986 \
  --data-parallel-size 2 \
  --data-parallel-backend mp \
  --max-model-len 4096 \
  --max-num-batched-tokens 4096 \
  --max-num-seqs 16 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.15 \
  --dtype bfloat16 \
  --seed 256 \
  --compilation-config '{"cudagraph_mode":"NONE"}' \
  --speculative-config "{\"model\":\"$MODEL_ID\",\"revision\":\"$MODEL_REVISION\",\"method\":\"draft_model\",\"num_speculative_tokens\":3}"
```

Start once with fresh cache directories, stop after startup/serving, then run
the identical command again without deleting the caches. On the pinned main
baseline `494663940b9b44f667c4f61c8c2407ba8e725ceb`, the warm restart fails with
`CUDA driver error: invalid argument`; at PR commit
`b2303c5e49471603cd31c1904352ad7d99164dbd`, cold and warm starts both serve.
The full raw logs retain the original local snapshot path so the executed argv
is not rewritten after the fact; the updated command uses the corresponding
public model revision.

GPU experiment: 2 H100 PCIe 80GB per arm, DP=2/MP, MRV2, BF16, compilation
enabled, CUDA graphs disabled. Both arms start with a fresh shared compilation
cache, then restart without removing it. The failure/fix was reproduced over
two separate cold/warm cycles per arm, with nonzero speculative acceptance on
both replicas. The 16-request smoke outputs, finish reasons and token counts
match across successful arms.

Full GSM8K (`lm_eval` 0.4.13, 5-shot, 1,319 questions, greedy, seed 256):
default-mode accuracy was **41.39% baseline vs 40.71% PR**. Unchanged-baseline
repeats also varied (48/128 vs 46/128; prefix cache not reset). A separate
`VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1` comparison produced identical responses for all 1,319
questions (40.33% each), with compilation still enabled. These controls do not
rule out a default-mode regression; all raw results are retained.

Three sequential `vllm bench serve` runs per arm used 128 prompts, input
256/output 128, concurrency 8, 16 warmups and fixed seed 256: **768 measured
requests and zero failures**. Shared GPU load and repeated prefix-cache effects
prevent an isolated-GPU speedup/non-regression claim.

Source is the full Python tree at main baseline
`494663940b9b44f667c4f61c8c2407ba8e725ceb` and PR
`b2303c5e49471603cd31c1904352ad7d99164dbd`, using official nightly
native/build-supplied files from parent
`3c13653738dad0acd877c23373816fefffbdd373` (PyTorch 2.14.0+cu130, Python
3.12.13). Native-source files do not change between the wheel parent and
baseline; CUDA kernels were not rebuilt. This is not a claim about the latest
moving main. Both arms disable the unavailable optional FlashInfer
sampler/toolchain. Same-model serving/cache validation does not establish
different-draft quality or broader model coverage.

## Details

Independent dense DP stores replica identity in `data_parallel_index` while its
distributed DP rank is reset to zero. Constructing the draft config with
`replace` reconstructs the parallel config and resets the index. Restoring the
target index before `get_model` gives distinct `rank_0_0`/`rank_0_1` draft
caches. No steady-state inference operation or synchronization is added.

AI assistance was used for implementation and to execute/document these
validations. The detailed results were collected by the agent and do not
represent independent human-run H100 validation.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][Rust Frontend] Read the text config under `thinker_config`
commits.pr_body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

The Rust frontend now finds the text config under `thinker_config`, so Qwen2.5-Omni, Qwen3-Omni and Qwen3-ASR checkpoints no longer fail at startup with "the model config does not define `vocab_size`". Fixes part 2 of #61057.

## Claims

- `VLLM_USE_RUST_FRONTEND=1 vllm serve Qwen/Qwen2.5-Omni-3B` starts and serves requests without `--hf-overrides`; before this change it exits during startup.
- Same for Qwen3-ASR once a `tokenizer.json` is present (the missing `tokenizer.json` is part 1 of #61057 and is not addressed here).
- `vocab_size`, `eos_token_ids`, `model_type` and the expert count (`is_moe`) now come from the same config Python's `get_text_config()` returns for these models. Top-level values still take precedence, so `--hf-overrides` behaves as before.

## Validation

Unit tests (Linux, Rust 1.95.0):

```
cargo test -p vllm-text --lib backend::hf::config
test result: ok. 14 passed; 0 failed
```

End to end on one A40 (driver 580.159.04), with the Rust frontend built from the base commit and from this change against the same Python install:

```
VLLM_USE_RUST_FRONTEND=1 VLLM_RUST_FRONTEND_PATH=<vllm-rs> \
  vllm serve <model> --max-model-len 4096 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85
```

| Model | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Qwen/Qwen2.5-Omni-3B` (ships `tokenizer.json`) | Rust frontend exits: `tokenizer error: the model config does not define vocab_size` | Starts; `/v1/chat/completions` "What is the capital of France? Answer in one word." (temperature 0) returns `Paris` |
| `Qwen/Qwen3-ASR-0.6B` + `tokenizer.json` saved from `AutoTokenizer` | Same error | Starts; `/v1/models` responds |

Validated on `3fe917abb` (the newest main commit with a published precompiled wheel at the time). This branch is rebased onto a later main; nothing under `rust/` changed between the two.

<details>
<summary>Startup log excerpts</summary>

Before:
```
(RustFrontend) INFO [hf.rs:227] loading tokenizer with fastokens path=.../Qwen2.5-Omni-3B/.../tokenizer.json
(RustFrontend) ERROR [cmd/src/main.rs:110] process failed with error: failed to create chat/text backends
  tokenizer error: the model config does not define `vocab_size`
RuntimeError: Frontend process failed during engine core initialization.
```

After:
```
INFO [utils.py:372] Launching Rust frontend: /root/vllm-rs-fix frontend ...
{"choices":[{"message":{"role":"assistant","content":"Paris"},"finish_reason":"stop"}], ...}
```
</details>

Not tested: `vllm-rs serve` with data parallelism on Qwen3-Omni (see Details).

## Details

**Root cause.** These configs nest the language model config two levels deep:

```
{ "model_type": "qwen3_asr",
  "thinker_config": { "audio_config": {...}, "text_config": { "vocab_size": 151936, ... } } }
```

`ModelConfig` in `rust/src/text/src/backend/hf/config.rs` only looks at the top level and `text_config` (alias `llm_config`). On the Python side, `Qwen3ASRConfig.get_text_config()` (and the transformers configs for Qwen2.5-Omni / Qwen3-Omni) return `thinker_config.text_config`, which is why the Python frontend works.

**Change.** Treat `thinker_config` as another alias of `text_config` (next to `llm_config`), and make `effective_text_config()` follow nested text configs to the innermost one. `vocab_size()`, `eos_token_ids()` and `model_type()` already recurse into `text_config`, so they reach `thinker_config.text_config` without further changes. Top-level values still win, so every config that worked before resolves the same way. A config with both a top-level `text_config` and a `thinker_config` would be rejected as a duplicate field; none of the Qwen2.5-Omni, Qwen3-Omni or Qwen3-ASR checkpoints has both. `talker_config` is not followed.

**Side effect worth reviewing.** For Qwen3-Omni, `num_experts` (128) also lives under the thinker, so `is_moe()` changes from false to true. In `vllm-rs serve`, that value decides whether the in-process DP coordinator is started (`rust/src/server/src/config.rs`). The new value matches what the Python engine computes, but I have only reasoned about this from the code and have not run Qwen3-Omni with DP > 1.

**Not in this PR.** Part 1 of #61057 (no `tokenizer.json` in the official Qwen3-ASR / Qwen3-Omni repos). I asked in the issue whether a clearer error or building the tokenizer from `vocab.json`/`merges.txt` is preferred.

**Duplicate check.** No open PR references #61057. #60979 touches the same model family but only the Python side (`qwen3_asr.py`, ragged audio batches).

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][Rust Frontend] Use prefiller cache hits for P/D usage
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose
Fix `usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens` in Rust P/D responses.

The decoder currently counts KV received from the prefiller as cached tokens. That can make a cold request look fully cached, even though the prefiller computed the entire prompt.

The Python frontend already handles this through `remote_prefill_cached_tokens` (#54222). This change reads the same metadata in Rust and uses it for response usage:

- Use the prefiller's count when `do_remote_prefill` is `true`, including an explicit zero. The parameters are read through a small typed view, so a non-boolean flag or a count that is not a non-negative integer leaves the decoder's count in place.
- Keep the existing decoder count when no usable override is available.
- Include `cached_tokens: 0` when prompt-token details are enabled. This also applies to ordinary local requests.
- Keep decoder metrics based on the raw engine statistics.

No new wire fields or prompt-length upper clamp are added.

Related-work searches found no matching open Rust fix. #58730 proposes bounds handling in Python; #56318 concerns cache-source metrics.

## Test Plan
From `rust/`:

```bash
cargo test --locked -p vllm-llm -p vllm-server --lib --tests
cargo clippy --locked -p vllm-llm -p vllm-server --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo fmt --all -- --check
git diff --check
```
The added tests cover metadata parsing, positive and zero overrides, missing-count fallback, streamed and collected usage, unchanged decoder metrics, and explicit-zero JSON serialization.

## Test Result
Validated against `a9eafde59cbd`:

- The mock-engine regression fails without the fix and passes with it.
- 454 tests passed: 15 LLM unit, 11 LLM integration, and 428 server tests.
- Clippy, formatting, and diff checks passed.

Also tested with real NIXL transfers on two H100 GPUs using Qwen3-0.6B. Across chat and completions, streaming and non-streaming, eight baseline cases reproduced the bug and eight patched cases reported the correct prefiller count. Detailed setup and results are in the follow-up comment.

This PR was written in part with the assistance of generative AI.

commits.pr_title: [Rust Frontend] Make HTTP request body limit configurable via VLLM_HTTP_MAX_REQUEST_BODY_SIZE
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

The Rust frontend caps HTTP request bodies at a fixed 32 MiB, introduced in #46582. The Python frontend (uvicorn) has no body-size limit, so long-context or batched requests that work fine against the Python server fail with a terminal client error on the Rust one (the length-limit rejection surfaces as a non-retryable 400). Anyone running long-prompt workloads or benchmark harnesses against the Rust frontend hits this divergence.

This PR keeps the 32 MiB default chosen in #46582 (which presumably has DoS resistance in mind) but makes the limit overridable via a `VLLM_HTTP_MAX_REQUEST_BODY_SIZE` environment variable (bytes); `0` removes the limit, matching the Python frontend. Like `VLLM_LOG_STATS_INTERVAL`, it is read once in `SharedRuntimeArgs` (a hidden env-bound flag for `vllm-rs serve`, and `apply_env_fallbacks` for the `--args-json` bootstrap path used by `vllm serve`), so an invalid value fails startup instead of silently keeping the default. The limit is carried in `ApiServerOptions` and applied by the HTTP API router; the standalone render router and gRPC keep the 32 MiB default. The env var is registered in `envs.py` for documentation and added to `compile_factors()`'s ignored factors, like `VLLM_HTTP_TIMEOUT_KEEP_ALIVE`.

## Duplicate-work check

No open PR or issue proposes making this limit configurable or raising it. Searched `gh pr list`/`gh issue list` on vllm-project/vllm for "json body limit", "body size rust", and related keywords; the only prior work is #46582 itself, which introduced the cap this PR parameterizes.

## Test Plan

- New test `chat_completions_reject_request_body_above_configured_limit`: a router built with a 1 KiB limit rejects a larger request with 400 and a length-limit error message.
- New test `chat_completions_accept_request_body_above_default_limit_when_unlimited`: with the limit removed, a body one byte over 32 MiB is accepted.
- The `vllm-cmd` env-setting tests cover the default, an override, `0` (no limit) and invalid values on both the `vllm-rs serve` and `--args-json` paths.
- Existing test `chat_completions_accepts_request_body_larger_than_axum_default` (from #46582) still passes, confirming the default is unchanged.

```
cargo test -p vllm-server -p vllm-cmd
cargo clippy -p vllm-server -p vllm-cmd --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo fmt --all --check
```

## Test Result

All `vllm-server` (511) and `vllm-cmd` (92) tests pass; clippy and rustfmt clean; pre-commit hooks (ruff, mypy, etc.) pass on the `envs.py` change.

## AI assistance disclosure

This PR was developed with AI assistance (Claude Code). I have reviewed every changed line and run the tests above.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][DCP] Finalize the NIXL DCP interleave size before profiling
commits.pr_body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

NIXL P/D + DCP resolved the KV-cache interleave after profiling, allowing sparse indexers and compiled graphs to consume a stale value. Resolve global cache groups first, finalize interleave once in the engine core, and assign the resolved value on workers before profiling.

Builds on the root-cause analysis and global-group approach in #60671 by @andylolu2, and incorporates @LucasWilkinson's [suggestion](https://github.com/NickLucche/vllm/pull/13). This updates the existing alternative PR; it retains the legacy interleave field and CLI behavior that #60671 removes.

## Claims

- The engine builds global KV-cache groups before profiling and reuses them for final allocation.
- `VllmConfig.finalize_kv_cache_layout` resolves NIXL DCP interleave once in the engine core. `set_kv_cache_layout(layout_name, cp_kv_cache_interleave_size)` sends the resolved values to workers, which only assign them.
- Connector initialization no longer adjusts interleave. Sparse indexers read the shared configuration directly instead of maintaining a separate lazy cache.

## Validation

**Current revision, CPU:** 85 tests passed, including the new core-to-worker startup test with different worker block sizes and an explicit interleave override, plus empty-group handling. All pre-commit hooks passed on the combined changed files, including mypy and test-CI tethering.

```bash
VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=cpu .venv/bin/python -m pytest -q \
  tests/v1/engine/test_kv_cache_group_metadata.py \
  tests/test_config.py::test_pd_dcp_interleave_size_is_adjusted_to_block_size \
  tests/test_config.py::test_kv_offloading_does_not_adjust_dcp_interleave_size \
  tests/test_config.py::test_finalizing_empty_kv_cache_layout_preserves_interleave \
  tests/v1/core/test_kv_cache_planning.py \
  tests/v1/core/test_kv_cache_config_builder.py \
  tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_kv_connector_lifecycle.py
```

**GPU serving/model evaluation has not been rerun for the global-group revision.** The results below validate the earlier worker-local revision and are retained as historical evidence. A NIXL + DCP serving rerun is still required for the updated startup flow. The new CPU tests run through the existing V1 Engine CI step; they do not replace GPU validation.

<details>
<summary>Earlier revision: GPU reproducer and model evaluation</summary>

GLM-5.3-Flash (`glm5next`, MRV2), real weights, 1x GB300 node, TP4 + DCP4, NIXL `kv_both`, GSM8K 5-shot, 1319 questions:

| Build | Configuration | Result |
|---|---|---|
| main (`e80b6c642f`) | Automatic interleave | Startup fails: compressed indexer requires interleave to be a multiple of 4; profiling still sees 1 |
| main (`e80b6c642f`) | Explicit `--cp-kv-cache-interleave-size 4` | 0.921 |
| Earlier worker-local revision of this PR | Automatic interleave resolved to 4 before profiling | 0.920 |

```bash
VLLM_SSM_CONV_STATE_LAYOUT=DS vllm serve zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash \
  --tensor-parallel-size 4 --decode-context-parallel-size 4 \
  --max-model-len 8192 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 --language-model-only \
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"NixlConnector","kv_role":"kv_both"}'
.venv/bin/python tests/evals/gsm8k/gsm8k_eval.py --port 8000
```

The earlier dummy-weight `DeepseekV3ForCausalLM` reproducer (`index_topk`, TP2 + DCP2, NIXL `kv_both`, compilation mode 0 and `FULL_DECODE_ONLY` graphs) observed indexer/metadata values of 1/64 during serving on main, versus 64/64 with early finalization. Its tokens/logprobs matched an explicit-interleave workaround. Dummy weights did not measure accuracy impact.

</details>

## Details

Startup order:

1. Load models and update backend block sizes.
2. Resolve the layout and global cache groups in the engine.
3. Finalize interleave once in the engine using the global groups, then send the resolved layout and interleave to workers for assignment before profiling.
4. Profile memory; allocate from the previously computed global groups.
5. Initialize the connector and capture serving graphs.

The existing layout RPC carries the resolved interleave alongside the layout name. The core owns resolution; workers assign the value to their existing `ParallelConfig`, preserving model-held references. Global groups stay in the core for final allocation. No additional RPC or configuration field is introduced.

The temporary KV cache used for CUDA-graph memory profiling still uses the model runners' existing local grouping. The core reuses its global groups for interleave resolution and final allocation; it does not redesign temporary profiling allocation or synchronize separate draft-model config copies.

Out-of-tree `set_kv_cache_layout` overrides must accept the resolved interleave argument. The legacy `dcp_kv_cache_interleave_size` field and its current precedence rules are retained.

commits.pr_title: [Kernel] Allow registering OOT block-scaled FP8 linear kernels
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Lets out-of-tree platforms register block-scaled FP8 linear kernels by adding `kernel_type="fp8_block"` to `register_linear_kernel`.

## Claims

- `register_linear_kernel(..., kernel_type="fp8_block")` adds the kernel to `_POSSIBLE_FP8_BLOCK_KERNELS`.
- OOT platforms can now serve `--quantization fp8_per_block`, which previously failed during kernel selection because the OOT platform had no entry in the block-kernel list.
- The docstring now lists every `kernel_type` the function accepts. It previously listed only `mp`, `int8` and `fp8`.

## Validation

- `pre-commit` passes (ruff, mypy, typos, SPDX).
- The change adds one `elif` branch that matches the existing `fp8`, `mxfp8`, `nvfp4`, `mxfp4` and `mxfp6` branches. Existing kernel types behave as before.

## Details

`Fp8PerBlockOnlineLinearMethod` (and `Fp8LinearMethod` with `block_quant`) use a `GroupShape(1, 128)` activation key. Because `is_per_group()` is true for that shape, `init_fp8_linear_kernel` picks the kernel from `_POSSIBLE_FP8_BLOCK_KERNELS`. That dict only has entries for CUDA, ROCm, CPU and XPU, and `register_linear_kernel` had no way to add to it. An OOT platform that registered its FP8 kernel with `kernel_type="fp8"` therefore got per-tensor and per-channel FP8 but never block-wise.

To support both, an OOT plugin registers the same class twice, once as `"fp8"` and once as `"fp8_block"`. If that class subclasses `FP8ScaledMMLinearKernel`, the block path already builds it with `layer_param_names` (see the `issubclass` branch in `init_fp8_linear_kernel`), so no new base class or interface change is needed.

commits.pr_title: [Kernel][Perf] Add H100 tuned configs for Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B to the batch-invariant matmul table
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

In short: in batch-invariant (BI) mode (`VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1`), every bf16 linear layer and the lm_head run the Triton kernel `matmul_kernel_persistent` instead of cuBLAS. Its tile comes from a per-GPU table, and the Hopper table only has the five Qwen3-1.7B shapes (measured on an H20), so Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B run the default 128x128x64 tile on H100. This PR adds H100-measured entries for their 8 TP=1 shapes to the `"hopper"` family.

With BI on, on an H100 SXM:
- `vllm bench latency` is 1.85-2.79x faster than main.
- The BI tax (latency with BI on / latency with BI off) drops from 2.13-2.99x on main to 1.03-1.20x with this PR.
- GSM8K stays within 0.5 standard error (SE) of main.

Related: tracker [#27433](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/27433), same kind of table as [#53247](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53247), [#57456](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57456), [#58495](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58495).

## Key results

- 8 new `(N, K)` entries in `_BATCH_INVARIANT_MATMUL_TUNED_CONFIGS["hopper"]`: gate_up/down/lm_head of Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B plus their shared qkv/o. Existing entries and other families are not touched.
- One `BLOCK_K` per shape, so a row's K-reduction order does not depend on M. Checked bit for bit through the real `matmul_persistent` dispatch: 2028/2028 cases identical.
- Kernel (H100 SXM, cold L2): geomean 2.03x vs main over 80 (shape, M) cases, 2.89x at M <= 64; the slowest case is 1.00x (Qwen3 gate_up at M=2048, 827 vs 828 us). At M <= 64 the kernel is now 0.90-1.12x of cuBLAS time (main: 1.48-4.09x).
- E2E latency with the flag on (fresh process per run, 2 interleaved rounds):

| model, workload | BI=0 (s) | BI=1 main (s) | BI=1 this PR (s) | PR vs main | BI tax main -> PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Llama-3.1-8B, 32 in / 128 out, bs 8 | 0.854 | 2.452 | 0.881 | 2.78x | 2.87x -> 1.03x |
| Llama-3.1-8B, 1024 in / 32 out, bs 8 | 0.403 | 0.859 | 0.444 | 1.94x | 2.13x -> 1.10x |
| Qwen3-8B, 32 in / 128 out, bs 8 | 0.893 | 2.668 | 0.956 | 2.79x | 2.99x -> 1.07x |
| Qwen3-8B, 1024 in / 32 out, bs 8 | 0.414 | 0.917 | 0.495 | 1.85x | 2.22x -> 1.20x |

- `vllm bench serve` (1024 in / 128 out, 1000 prompts, rate inf, 3 interleaved rounds, req/s; rounds 1 / 2 / 3, then the mean). Llama-3.1-8B gains 13.6%. Qwen3-8B does not change; Details explains why (the execution mode these shapes switch on, not the tiles).

| model | BI=0 | BI=1 main | BI=1 this PR | PR vs main | throughput tax main -> PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Llama-3.1-8B | 28.29 / 28.35 / 28.32, 28.32 | 21.62 / 21.69 / 21.61, 21.64 | 24.71 / 24.57 / 24.48, 24.59 | +13.6% | 1.31x -> 1.15x |
| Qwen3-8B | 27.43 / 27.47 / 27.54, 27.48 | 21.45 / 21.48 / 21.51, 21.48 | 21.50 / 21.48 / 21.47, 21.48 | 0.0% | 1.28x -> 1.28x |

- GSM8K (5-shot, BI=1): every difference to main is within 0.5 SE.

| model | main strict / flexible | this PR strict / flexible |
|---|---|---|
| Llama-3.1-8B | 0.7180 ± 0.0124 / 0.7832 ± 0.0114 | 0.7119 ± 0.0125 / 0.7839 ± 0.0113 |
| Qwen3-8B | 0.8764 ± 0.0091 / 0.8779 ± 0.0090 | 0.8741 ± 0.0091 / 0.8757 ± 0.0091 |

The raw output for every row of these tables is under Validation.

## Validation

**Setup.**
- GPU: 1x H100 80GB HBM3 SXM, 132 SMs, power limit 700 W of 700 W.
- Software: driver 595.91.07, CUDA 13.0, torch 2.14.0+cu130, triton 3.8.0.
- main = 307c5844ad. PR = main + this commit, applied on the box with `git am` (same diff).
- main and PR are the same checkout, switched with `git checkout`. Every run is a fresh process.
- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct checkpoint: `unsloth/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct`, an ungated copy. It has the same architecture and layer shapes as `meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct`; its config.json adds `pad_token_id`. I did not compare the weights against the gated repo.
- [#61118](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/61118) merged after this base. It enables Inductor's `batch_invariant` flag. It can only change the torch.compile arms (main, and PR + torch.compile under Details). It does not change this PR's default breakable-graph mode, because that mode does not run Inductor.

**Bitwise.**
- Path: `matmul_persistent` on the PR tree, all 13 hopper shapes.
- Check: a probe row at rows 0, M/2 and M-1 must equal the same row computed at M=1.
- M values (39): 1-17, every bucket edge ±1, 100, 1000, 3000 and 4096.
- 2 seeds. Weight as `w.t()` (the linear layout) and as a contiguous `(K, N)` tensor.
- Result: 2028/2028 identical, 0 mismatched.

**Tests** (PR tree):

```
pytest -v tests/v1/determinism/test_matmul_batch_invariant.py                                  # 35 passed, 2 skipped
VLLM_TEST_MODEL=Qwen/Qwen3-8B pytest -v tests/v1/determinism/test_batch_invariance.py            # 22 passed
```

- The launches cycle over enough weight copies to read >= 4x L2 per pass.
- main is the mean of two runs, one before and one after the PR run. The two runs agree within 0.98-1.08x.

**Latency** (`vllm bench latency`):

## Details

**These shapes also change the execution mode.**
- Since [#57586](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57586), BI mode checks the model's qkv/o/gate_up/down shapes against the device's table.
- If one shape is in the table (bf16, unquantized, CUDA, not `enforce_eager`, `VLLM_USE_BREAKABLE_CUDAGRAPH` unset), the model runs with breakable CUDA graphs and without torch.compile.
- In that mode the tile is looked up from the runtime M. Under torch.compile the lookup is frozen to one tile at trace time ([#54243](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/54243)).
- So this PR moves Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B to breakable graphs, in addition to the new tiles.

To separate the two effects, I ran two extra arms, 1 round each (raw output in the "mode diagnostic" dropdown under Validation):
- main + breakable graphs (`VLLM_USE_BREAKABLE_CUDAGRAPH=1`): the mode change only.
- PR + torch.compile (`VLLM_USE_BREAKABLE_CUDAGRAPH=0`): the new tiles. qkv/o/gate_up/down are frozen to one tile; lm_head runs outside the compiled forward and keeps the per-M lookup.

| model | arm | latency 32/128 (s) | latency 1024/32 (s) | serve (req/s) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Llama-3.1-8B | main | 2.452 | 0.859 | 21.64 |
| Llama-3.1-8B | main + breakable graphs | 2.423 | 0.856 | 21.34 |
| Llama-3.1-8B | PR + torch.compile | 1.824 | 0.667 | 24.81 |
| Llama-3.1-8B | PR (default: breakable graphs) | 0.881 | 0.444 | 24.59 |
| Qwen3-8B | main | 2.668 | 0.917 | 21.48 |
| Qwen3-8B | main + breakable graphs | 2.639 | 0.926 | 20.30 |
| Qwen3-8B | PR + torch.compile | 2.120 | 0.763 | 22.66 |
| Qwen3-8B | PR (default: breakable graphs) | 0.956 | 0.495 | 21.48 |

What the table shows:
- The gain comes from the tiles. Breakable graphs alone change latency by about 1%.
- Per-M tile selection makes decode fast: 0.881 s, against 1.824 s with one frozen tile.
- In all four latency workloads, breakable graphs win by 1.5-2.2x.
- In the prefill-heavy serve workload, torch.compile wins:
  - Dropping Inductor costs 5.5% on Qwen3-8B and 1.4% on Llama-3.1-8B.
  - With breakable graphs, the new tiles only win back that 5.5% on Qwen3-8B.
  - PR + torch.compile is ahead by 5.5% (Qwen3-8B) and 0.9% (Llama-3.1-8B), 1 round each.
- This trade-off comes from the [#57586](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57586) gate, not from these entries. I did not change the gate.
- With this table, `VLLM_USE_BREAKABLE_CUDAGRAPH=0` gives Qwen3-8B serving +5.5% over main.

**How the entries were picked.**
- Search space and BLOCK_K rule are the same as [#57456](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57456):
  - BLOCK_K {32, 64, 128} x BLOCK_M {16, 32, 64, 128} x BLOCK_N {32, 64, 128, 256} x warps {4, 8} x stages {2, 3, 4, 5}.
  - Timed at M in {1, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 256, 512, 1024, 2048}.
  - One BLOCK_K per shape, by the decode-weighted score. Then the fastest tile per bucket with that BLOCK_K.
- Two differences from [#57456](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57456):
  - Cold-L2 timing. Each point is a CUDA graph that cycles over enough copies of `(x, w)` to read >= 4x L2 per pass. o (32 MB) and qkv (48 MB) fit in the 50 MB L2, so warm timing would make them look faster than in the model.
  - The bitwise gate runs on all 10 buckets, not 4. A probe row at rows 0, M/2 and M-1 must equal the M=1 output.
- Before the gate, the top 3 configs per (bucket, BLOCK_K) were re-timed over 5 interleaved passes.
- Margins:
  - 43 of 80 picks beat the runner-up by more than the pass-to-pass spread.
  - The other 37 are within the spread. 20 of them are within 1%. The rest are at M >= 256, where the spread is larger.
  - Every pick is faster than main's default tile. In 77 of 80 buckets the margin is larger than the spread; the other 3 are 1.04-1.07x.
- Result: BLOCK_K = 64 for Llama gate_up, 128 for the other 7 shapes.

**Not a duplicate.**
- [#60034](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/60034) (draft) tunes five other Hopper shapes (17408x5120, 5120x8704, 8192x5120, 5120x3072, 124160x5120) for M <= 16. No overlap.
- [#54503](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54503) and [#55752](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/55752) change how the M bucket is selected at runtime. They work with any table entries.
- [#59952](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59952) (split-K for N <= 64) replaces the table lookup in `matmul_persistent` with a fixed heuristic. If it lands as written today, these entries and the existing Ada/Hopper/Blackwell/SM120 entries no longer set the tile. The [#57586](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57586) gate still reads the table, so they would still switch the execution mode.
- [#53446](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53446) (closed) proposed H100 NVL configs for the Qwen3-1.7B shapes already in the table. This PR adds new shapes only. It does not change existing entries.

**Limitations.**
- Measured on H100 SXM only. The `"hopper"` key also covers H100 PCIe/NVL, H200, H800 and H20. For these shapes they run the default tile today. I have not measured them.
- With these entries, the jit monitor logged at most one `matmul_kernel_persistent` compile per process. In latency and serve runs it came during warmup, never in a measured iteration (none in the Llama decode latency runs). In lm_eval, which has no warmup, it came on the first request; that changes timing only, not scores. main logged none.
- TP > 1 per-rank shapes are not included.
- The table and the [#57586](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57586) gate use only `(N, K)`. Other bf16 models with the same shapes also get these tiles and the mode change. Example: Mistral-7B-v0.3 has exactly the layer shapes of Llama-3.1-8B. I have not measured those models.
- CI: the H100 Batch Invariance job runs `test_batch_invariance.py` (Qwen3-1.7B, plus needle tests on DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8) and the RMSNorm and LoRA-shrink tests. It does not run `test_matmul_batch_invariant.py`, and none of its models use these shapes. So only the validation above covers these entries.

I used Claude Code for this change. I reviewed every line and ran the tests and benchmarks above myself.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix] Initialize valid ModelOpt NVFP4 MoE dummy scales
commits.pr_body:
## Overview Initialize ModelOpt NVFP4 MoE dummy quantization scales to valid positive values. Random initialization could produce nonpositive block/input scales and inconsistent gate/up global scales when benchmarking with `--load-format dummy`. ## Claims - Dummy NVFP4 MoE weights use positive scales and matching gate/up global scales through the existing `dummy_weight_value` loader contract. - A regression test constructs a small Qwen3 MoE through `LLM`, confirms the FlashInfer TRTLLM backend and valid scales, and generates two tokens with finite returned log probabilities. - The ModelOpt documentation explains dummy benchmarking and the FlashInfer MegaMoE backend flag. ## Validation One GB200 GPU, BF16 activations, NVFP4 dummy experts, FlashInfer TRTLLM, eager execution: | Check | Without fix | With fix | | --- | --- | --- | | `test_modelopt_nvfp4_dummy_scales` | Failed: `AssertionError: w13_weight_scale` at `assert (values > 0).all()` | 1 passed, 22 deselected; two generated tokens and finite returned log probabilities | The same test command was run with the production change removed and restored: ```bash CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 HF_HOME=/mnt/lustre/hf-models \ .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/quantization/test_blackwell_moe.py \ -k test_modelopt_nvfp4_dummy_scales -x -v -s ``` Relevant before/after output: ```text Before: AssertionError: w13_weight_scale assert tensor(False, device='cuda:0') 1 failed, 22 deselected, 1 warning in 15.15s After: 1 passed, 22 deselected, 1 warning in 16.22s ``` The test runs in the existing B200 Quantized MoE Buildkite step, whose dependencies already cover both changed Python files. ```bash .venv/bin/pre-commit run --files \ vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/modelopt.py \ tests/quantization/test_blackwell_moe.py \ docs/features/quantization/modelopt.md git diff --check ``` Both passed, including Ruff, mypy, Markdown lint, and test tethering. A fresh-agent local-checkout documentation search found and quoted the dummy benchmarking section. A separate real-LLM smoke run on this PR checkout also passed with two GB200 GPUs, TP2/EP2, the same tiny Qwen3 MoE configuration, and `moe_backend="flashinfer_moe_ep_cutedsl"`: two generated tokens with finite log probabilities. This uses the native dummy loader, without a benchmark wrapper. No real-checkpoint quality evaluation was run: this change only supplies values consumed by dummy weight initialization, and dummy outputs are unsuitable for quality evaluation. ## Details The generic dummy initializer samples floating-point values around zero. NVFP4 MoE quantization scales require positive values, and the fused gate/up projections share a global scale. The change assigns block scales `1.0`, global weight scales `1e-3`, and input scales `1e-2` using parameter metadata already supported by the loader. It adds no inference-time work; normal checkpoint loading continues to use checkpoint values. Duplicate-work searches on 2026-10-26 for `ModelOpt dummy`, `NVFP4 scales`, `MegaMoE dummy`, and `"dummy_weight_value"` found no open PR implementing this dummy initialization fix. Related #55073 reconciles differing scales in real checkpoints, #45320 rejects missing checkpoint scales, and #55997 refactors ModelOpt MoE methods; they address different behavior. There is no associated issue. AI assistance was used to implement, validate, review, and document this change. ---
